Mydei wakes to the lingering impression of Phainon beside him. He blinks in the dim light and reaches out, brushing over the still-warm divots in the sheets. The absence takes a moment to register, his thoughts sluggish and slow to form. He’s used to waking with Phainon in his arms or tucked up around his back. The lack of his familiar weight is disconcerting.

He sits up. Outside, the morning draws a faint outline of Okhema’s skyline. It’s earlier than when they usually rise. The absence of the Dawn Device is still a significant adjustment.

He rubs the sleep out of his eyes, focuses and—there. His husband sits at the foot of the bed with various scrolls spread around him, illuminated by a lit bronze lamp on a nearby low table. He’s wearing a short chiton that must be one of Mydei’s, hemmed in red and black. Beagle Coconut is curled up in a fluffy ball on his lap while Honey Fruitcake nestles into his side, his upper body draped across Phainon’s leg and nose buried in Beagle Coconut’s fur.

Phainon reaches for a scroll. A few strands of hair fall into his eyes. He absently tucks them behind his ear. The lamplight pools in his collarbones, spills across his skin in soft amber, catching on each rhimágmata and every little scar, even the tips of the divots along his back where his wings would emerge if ever called.

Mydei’s fingers itch for his teleslate, or even a brush. He’s no talent for painting, but perhaps he can learn. For moments like these. They have time now, after all. Time for art and reading and slow mornings. Time to create what the world no longer demands they destroy.

He shifts, familiar with but still unprepared for how full his chest suddenly feels. Phainon looks over his shoulder. His eyes wrinkle with a smile. “Hi, good morning. I was trying to be quiet. Did I wake you?”

“You didn’t,” Mydei says gruffly. He stays where he is, resisting the urge to reach over and gather Phainon into his arms, if only to not disturb his reading. “You’re up already.” It’s a half-question.

Phainon shrugs, looking sheepish. “I felt too awake, for some reason.” He pats the space next to him. “Sit and read with me?”

Mydei is already slipping out from under the sheet. He carefully avoids the sleeping chimeras and settles beside his husband. If Beagle Coconut hadn’t taken his place on Phainon’s lap, he would have gladly laid his head there and let Phainon run his hands through his hair.

“Are you feeling unwell?” he asks, encircling Phainon’s bare knee with a gentle hand. “Do your legs still hurt?”

“Would you believe me if I say I feel better than ever?” Phainon replies. “That tonic you gave me worked wonders. I feel like I have enough energy to run a hundred laps around Okhema.”

“We’ll have to thank Demetria for the recipe,” Mydei says. “She gave us other ones to try. I’ll experiment with our breakfast today, if you can find it in yourself to not be so disappointed at the lack of olive relish.”

“You know I’ll never turn down anything you make.” The corners of Phainon’s lips lift. “Experiment or not. After all, was it not I who insisted on having the first taste of your— what did the twins call it—crystal lizard satay?”

Heat creeps up Mydei’s neck. That dish was a recipe Caelus and Stelle taught him from Jarilo-VI. They promised it would be a great pre-spar snack, going so far as to procure the main ingredients for him. After eating one, Phainon had landed in bed with a fever for several quints while Mydei sweated and swore over the worst stomach ache he had since his time in the wilds.

The blistering chase he gave the twins through Okhema once the pain became tolerable was lauded as one of the greatest displays of endurance and dexterity the citizens had seen. It has its own mural in the Court of Seasons.

“That,” he growls, “won’t happen again.”

Phainon rubs his back. “I doubt Demetria would give us anything like that. Actually,” he draws one of the scrolls closer, scanning it thoughtfully. “Everthing she gave us seem to have multiple uses, all good.”

“How so?” Mydei asks, getting comfortable for one of Phainon’s long winding explanations.

Phainon hums. “Did you know that in Oleinus, they brewed cremni pear and apple peel together into a tonic for expectant mothers? Helped ease muscle cramps in their first and second trimesters.”

Mydei chokes, tensing. Phainon startles and thumps on his back. “What,” Mydei croaks, willing his thymós to be calm, please, not a crystallization mishap in their private rooms of all places. “Expectant—expectant mothers?”

Phainon nods earnestly. “It was a tradition for pregnant women to drink one cup every day to relieve muscle aches. But its effects became so well regarded that even the soldiers of Oleinus and its neighboring city-states started using it for recovery after battles. Mydei, are you okay? Your face is pale.”

General use for muscle aches. It makes sense. Perfect, logical sense. There were many herbs and plants back in Kremnos used for all manner of things, pregnancy included, but nothing unusual about that, right?

Mydei takes a deep, steadying breath to collect his thoughts. “Fine, I’m fine. That’s interesting. I didn’t expect the tonic to have a maternal origin.”

Phainon chuckles. “I was caught off-guard as well. When I first read it, I thought,” he pauses. Something flickers in his eyes before it disappears under a bright smile. “I mean, I’m glad I was able to try it. It was delicious.”

Mydei swallows hard past the sudden lump in his throat. There it is again—the feeling at the base of his spine. “I’m glad. I… what else were you reading?”

He was never good at subtly changing the subject, but Phainon doesn’t seem to mind, relaxing into his side. He watches, throat still tight, as his husband rifles through the scrolls.

“There is this one book that Dan Heng gave me a few days ago. He mentioned it’s a copy of some academic texts from his homeland. His people are called the Vidyadhara. Apparently, they’re a long-life species who hatch from eggs after hundreds of years of molting…”

Mydei rests his head against Phainon’s shoulder and closes his eyes. He lets the sound of Phainon's voice wash over him. Wills the knot of heat and tension in his body to unravel quietly.

Moments like these are precious. He won’t let them be spoiled by…. Foolish inklings. Foolish thoughts of foolish things. So he sinks into the stories Phainon shares with him, of dragons and rebirth and mythical glowing eggs, and lets Phainon’s words carry him elsewhere.

They stay like that until dawn blooms over Okhema, oranges and yellows blending into the brightening blue. Phainon douses the lamp. Their room warms as the early breeze ruffles the scrolls and sheets. The chimeras stir awake.

Mydei watches through half-lidded eyes as Honey Fruitcake croons to Beagle Coconut, pawing at his flank. But instead of leaping on his mate in glee like he usually does in the morning, Beagle Coconut whines and firmly burrows his head into Phainon’s stomach.

Phainon makes a startled sound. “Hey now little one, what’s the matter?” The chimera squeaks in protest when he tries to lift him. “Huh. Someone’s clingy today.”

Honey Fruitcake chirrups loudly, trying to worm his way onto Phainon’s lap. Mydei can hear his worry but, “Behave,” he says and picks him up. One chimera is heavy enough, and Honey Fruitcake has particularly sharp claws. “Let him be. He’ll come to you when he’s ready. And you,” he tells Beagle Coconut, “watch where you’re putting those horns.”

Beagle Coconut’s responding apologetic croon is muffled by Phainon’s chiton. Honey Fruitcake, on the other hand, narrows his eyes and growls at Mydei as if personally insulted. Mydei stares him back down, unimpressed.

“He’s not going to gorge me,” Phainon chides. He runs his hands over Beagle Coconut, looking thoughtful. “Is it just me or is he getting rounder?”

Honey Fruitcake squeals, squirming so wildly that Mydei has to place him on the ground. “I wouldn’t be surprised, with how many snacks you give him when you think I’m not looking.”

“You know about that?” Phainon exclaims, clutching Beagle Coconut who also squeaks incredulously.

Mydei rolls his eyes. Phainon didn’t even try to deny it. “I know about it because I’m the one who makes those snacks for you in the first place.”

Phainon winces. “Looks like we’ve been found out, little one,” he says to Beagle Coconut, who lifts his head from Phainon’s belly with a curious awoo. Phainon scratches him under his chin. “Ready to face the day? Your partner’s waiting for you.”

Honey Fruitcake nearly shakes with impatience as Phainon gently sets a now docile Beagle Coconut on the floor. The moment his paws touch down, Honey Fruitcake tussles him to the ground and begins grooming him with rough and scolding sounds. Beagle Coconut bats him away, barking, and there they go, rolling around and nipping playfully at each other.

Mydei thinks, now that is an excellent idea, and turns to his husband. Phainon is smiling, watching the chimeras play-fight. Then their eyes lock, and he flushes in unmistakable understanding.

“Mydei,” he says, scrambling further up the kline. Then, louder but no less delighted as Mydei advances, “Mydeimos, the chimeras—”

“Already have a head start,” Mydei says gravely, and tackles him into the sheets. After, when he’s aching in the best way and luxuriating in how Phainon gazes down at him in pleasure and happiness, Mydei pulls him down and murmurs against his lips, “Phainon, good morning.”

Much later, their teleslates buzz in unison, breaking the peaceful quiet. Phainon’s teleslate rattles so much it falls off the kline.

“Did we miss something?” Phainon muses, pausing in his washing of Mydei’s hair.

Mydei, lazy and pliant under Phainon’s hands, frowns at the interruption. He reaches for his own teleslate and sighs at the numerous group chats waiting to be opened.

Phainon leans over his shoulder, his chest damp and warm. “Not good news?”

“We’ll see.” Mydei opens the messages and tilts the teleslate so Phainon can read at the same time.

Aglaea

See you at the baths

The Station wants to meet with Phainon and Tribios. I’ve attached a copy of their official request for your purview. I was able to negotiate the duration to a day only. Do keep a handle on that thymós of yours in the meantime.

Welt Yang

Everyone on the Express, please constantly keep in touch.

Good morning, Mydeimos. Lady Aglaea might have already told you about the situation. It’s ahead of schedule, but Madam Herta was insistent on meeting today. She mentioned a new parameter that she needs to analyze urgently.

We tried to ask for more information, but she can be evasive when she wants to be.

Himeko and I will be with Phainon and Tribios the whole time. I give you my word that they will be safe.

Chrysos Heirs

Cipher: Ugh, the Station is sooo boring to play in, but I did my part last time. It’s your turn now @Tribios @Phainon, do some nasty damage!

Aglaea: Do not do some nasty damage.

Tribios: I just got the message, see you at the Eschatheion, Snowy! Also De, don’t frown too much. You’ll scare the honor guards.

Anaxagoras: @Aglaea Stop ignoring my messages.

Aglaea: What a spectacular morning. The weather is sublime. The Eschatheion will look particularly bright today, don’t you all think?

Aglaea: Anyway. Teacher, Phainon, I’ve approved the request. Please be ready by Ascent Hour. Herta wants to start as soon as poosible.

Mydei must be making a ferocious face, because Phainon wraps his arms around him and kisses his cheek. “It can’t be helped,” Phainon says, extricating the teleslate from Mydei’s grip.

“The one they want is you. They’re only asking for Tribios out of courtesy,” Mydei replies sharply, tilting his head to give Phainon more room. “It’s insulting. You are not a dog the Station can just call on whenever they wish.”

Phainon chuckles, pressing little kisses down Mydei’s neck. He reaches the divot where it meets the shoulder and murmurs, “Woof.”

Ridiculous. Mydei fights the smile pulling at his lips. It shouldn’t be allowed, how quickly that settles his nerves. “They’ll keep you and Tribios for a day,” he says, turning to properly face Phainon. “Are you really okay with that?”

Phainon hums, linking their hands under the water. “Aglaea and the Trailblazers trust them. As peculiar as Madam Herta and the rest of the Station may be, I believe they’re doing their best to help us in the long run.”

“I question their intentions when they come at your expense,” Mydei says.

“It’s hardly an expense, compared to everything else I’ve done.”

Mydei says, low and firm, “Don’t measure it against the cycles. It’s not a fair comparison. And cease offering yourself like a sacrifice at an altar that no longer exists.”

It’s an old back-and-forth between them. Amphoreus, in its transformation from data to reality, had shattered cosmic rules they hadn’t known existed. That came with a cost beyond the ones Phainon bore on his skin, in his soul.

Until Amphoreus accumulates enough memoria to stabilize itself in the Cosmos, it is Phainon —out of all the Heirs—who will remain under the closest scrutiny from the Trailblazers’ Erudition allies. It is the unspoken agreement for their support, a temporary stopgate against the more dangerous interests of the Cosmos.

Mydei abhors the compromise, if it can even be called that. Gathering of memoria takes time, time no amount of Mydei’s fury or yearning can hasten. If he could, he would drag the stars into alignment himself to relieve his husband of another burden he shouldn’t have to carry.

Phainon’s eyes are soft and imploring as he rests his palm on Mydei’s cheek, thumb brushing over his tattoo. “Okay, okay,” he soothes, “I’ll speak to Caelus. See if he can help us leave sooner. He owes us that at least, with how much he riled you up yesterday.”

Mydei exhales. “Between him and Stelle, he was fine.” He leans into Phainon’s touch. “Though I question what goes in both their heads sometimes.”

“Perhaps he’ll tell you once he knows you won’t pummel him into the ground for, what did you say yesterday? Challenging your patience?”

“As if Dan Heng would even let me near him with my gauntlets.”

Phainon cackles. “You’ve noticed that too?”

Mydei gives him a pointed look and nips at his palm. “You don’t get to talk. You’re just as bad as he is.”

Phainon’s laugh mellows into something warmer and sweeter. “That’s how we are when we have someone precious to protect,” he says, rich with teasing affection. His gaze is a heavy, deliberate thing, settling on Mydei like silk sliding over bare skin.

Warmth floods Mydei’s face. It’s worse knowing Phainon can feel it.

He doesn’t need to be protected. It wasn’t a luxury afforded to him during his formative years. He’s long learned to live without it, hardened himself against the absence. But a deep, brutally honest part of him thrills in knowing he has Phainon’s. Not just his protection, but his devotion. Wholly. Unconditionally.

Mydei quickly looks away, the feel of Phainon’s hand lingering. The tips of his ears burn. His fingertips tingle. He wants his husband again, and not just once more. “HKS. Hurry up and bathe. You’re going to be late.”

It’s a weak retort, spoken hoarsely, but Phainon chooses to be magnanimous. He grins and presses a chaste kiss to Mydei’s cheek. “Come then, Mydeimos. Let’s not make the world wait any longer.”

“Snowy!” Tribios sweeps Phainon into her arms, squeezing tightly. “Look at you, aren’t you all spiffied up!”

“Thank you,” Phainon wheezes, “Lady Tribios, my ribs.”

She gasps, releasing him. “I’m sorry—I keep forgetting my strength. It's taking a while to get used to, you know, this.”

In her current state, she nearly rivals Mydei in height. Her scarlet hair cascades to below her waist, dotted throughout with flowers in multiples of three. She looks well, healthy and glowing.

“So handsome!” Tribios continues to gush, twirling her finger and giggling as Phainon indulges her with a dramatic spin. “What’s the occasion? If I had known we’d be dressing fancy, I’d have worn my nicer clothes!”

“Ask Mydei,” Phainon says dryly. “Apparently dressing myself is a threat to interstellar peace.”

Mydei’s side-eye could make stone sweat. He opens the gallery on his teleslate. “It might have been, with that awful himation you tried to sneak past me this morning.”

“It wasn’t that bad,” Phainon argues hopelessly as Tribios nearly laughs herself into tears over the photoslate Mydei shows her. “It wasn’t—I thought it would match the aesthetic of the Station!”

“It was seven different shades of gray,” Mydei stresses. He ushers them toward the Eschatheion, where a crowd is beginning to gather. “I do not wish to ask how you procured such a thing. At least you look somewhat respectable now.”

It’s a bit of an understatement. His husband has always been attractive. That was never in doubt, even when Mydei knew nothing of him except his skill with the sword, until years later when Phainon defied Destruction itself, golden-haloed and dark-winged and cleaving stars apart.

But now Phainon draws the eye far too easily in his new ensemble: gossamer gold and wine-dark robes swishing around his ankles, pauldron and armor polished to a shine. Twin plaits sweep back from his temples, secured with the gold clasp which matches the thick gold bands wrapped above each sizable bicep.

He looks regal. A kindly king, smiling and sure against the bright blue sky of Dawncloud.

Mydei’s chest suddenly tightens, conflicted between ferocious pride and the instinct to draw Phainon back to his side where they can keep each other safe. The sentiment only intensifies when the crowd bursts with giggles as Phainon waves at them.

He’s not jealous, truly. There is no reason for him to be, and never has been. That is his husband. His equal for life and whatever comes after. Okhema knows it, oddly enough revels in it.

But the Cosmos is an unfamiliar battlefield, with far too many unknowns, few allies, and even fewer friends. Phainon represents Amphoreus on a scale completely different to that of the Senate or the Council. In a few minutes, he’ll be leagues away from Okhema, from the other Heirs. From Mydei. Tribios is strong, so strong in her own way, but she cannot parse the intentions and ambitions of others in the martial way that Mydei can, were he able to go himself.

“Mydei,” Phainon calls, with a note of concern. He’s standing in front of the platform with Tribios and the honor guards. He points up. “They’re activating it.”

The crowd hushes as Mydei strides forward. Behind Phainon and Tribios, the Eschatheion— the Great Bridge Beyond the Sky—begins to materialize, a beam of pure white light that will take them to the stars where the Trailblazers will receive them safely.

Phainon gazes at him. “Alright?” It’s intimate enough, tender enough to make Mydei’s teeth ache.

He rips apart his foolish, floundering thoughts. So unbecoming. Phainon is not a sun that the stars may claim as one of their own. Not anymore.

The honor guards of the Eschatheion take one glance at Mydei’s face and look away politely. Tribios feigns admiration of a nearby statue. Several teleslates whip out among the crowd.

Mydei pays them little mind as he cups his husband’s face, mindful of the gauntlet’s sharp edges. “Be careful while you’re there. Call out to me should you need help.”

Phainon covers his hand with his own. “We’ll be fine. Just a day, and we’ll be right back.”

“Next time, I will be going with you,” Mydei declares. “It’s unwise to keep separating like this. We should not let the Station divide the Heirs as they please.”

“I’ll speak to the Trailblazers and Madam Herta,” Phainon says, nuzzling into Mydei’s palm. “We’ll have to think of something to give in return.”

A shadow must cross over Mydei’s expression, because Phainon adds gently, that only Mydei can hear, “You know we need the Station’s support until we can stand on our own. The Cosmos are watching and we’ve only just begun to rebuild. If we hesitate or falter now, they’ll see weakness.”

He’s not wrong. In the eyes of the stars, Amphoreus is a ripe fruit ready to be plucked and devoured. A fertile ground for exploration and experimentation. Or conquest. It was inevitable. Their world birthed a story that drew the gaze of not just one, but three Aeons. It was a blessing, a warning, and a divine reckoning all at once.

From what the crew of the Express told them, dozens of galactic systems are already in motion, hungry to stake their claim in the path Amphoreus would take.

Spurred by the thought, Mydei presses their foreheads together. The tips of their noses brush. His hand curls over the leather band covering the mark of the sun. Mydei says roughly, “Who is weak? Let them come. I’ll be glad to test their mettle and show them a taste of Strife.”

Amphoreus has guardians of its own, now, and stalwart allies along the silver rail. The Chrysos Heirs would never permit Amphoreus to sink back into the despair of fated cycles, and the Trailblazers would never permit them to face fate alone again.

Phainon smiles, eyes fluttering shut. He slips one arm around Mydei’s back. His palm, warm and broad, covers the tenth thoracic vertebra. “Careful now, Mydei. With such an open invitation, you might find a worthy opponent who’ll impress you even by your Kremnoan standards, and then what will I do?”

“Of all things, that is what you focused on?” Mydei scolds. He closes his eyes too. His hands slide from Phainon’s face to his waist, holding him close. “Do I worry myself like that when you have to meet with those men from the Xianzhou or Penacony? Concern yourself with finishing your mission in haste.”

“Why must I be in haste?” Phainon teases. “Don’t tell me the Guardian of Amphoreus is already itching for another spar? I didn’t think you’d be so eager to be handed another loss.”

“The Guardian of Amphoreus,” Mydei mimics in Phainon’s exact tone, drinking in the laugh Phainon gives out, “thinks that the Deliverer of Amphoreus should exert more effort in recalling exactly who got the final hit in during the last bout.”

“Mmm, was it perhaps me, when I got you on your back for the third time that day?”

Mydei tightens his grip as he husks, “If I remember correctly, it was you on your back that fourth time.”

Phainon draws back in surprise at his daring. His eyes widen briefly before darkening, half-lidded. It’s a look Mydei knows well, one that leads to heated tumbles behind closed doors or, on a few special occasions, their balcony, the Hero’s Bath at midnight, a particularly secluded corner of Kephale Square…

There’s a wave of muffled squeals and swoons from the crowd. Tribios clears her throat. The Eschatheion pulses impatiently, now a near solid panel of white light behind her and the blushing honor guards.

Mydei blinks. When had the Eschatheion fully activated? When did the crowd swell to nearly hundreds in number?

“Whoops,” Phainon says, not sounding the least bit sorry or surprised. He grins. “I win. You blinked first.”

Mydei scowls, mostly out of principle. “I’m still in the lead. By a wide margin, by the way.”

“Sure, if you’re deliberately don’t count the times when—”

“Snowy, De,” Tribios interrupts, obviously fighting her mirth. “We can’t delay anymore. You two can pick this up once we get back.”

Phainon gives her an apologetic smile, letting go of Mydei. “To be continued,” he says, a promise. “Duty calls.”

“Mm. Remember what I said.” Mydei lifts his chin, readying himself.

“Don’t I always?” Phainon winks and turns away to walk toward Tribios.

Mydei is left standing, lips slightly parted.

Which, what.

The crowd titters. Tribios covers her mouth. One of the honor guards, a Kremnoan, places his face in his palms.

What.

“HKS,” Mydei hisses, crossing the distance in loud stomps. His tattoos flare out bright and obvious.

Phainon glances over his shoulder, pretending to look confused. He’s not a good actor. His eyes glimmer with mischief, with a challenge. Come and get me.

Mydei seizes his shoulders, spins him around, and kisses him hard. With tongue. Sweet vengeance.

The crowd’s cheers are deafening.

“That,” Mydei snaps, licking his lips as he releases Phainon, “is how you do a proper farewell.”

“I see,” Phainon breathes, starry-eyed. “Maybe you can demonstrate again? Just one more time?”

Mydei shoves him into the middle of Eschatheion. Tribios glides into place next to Phainon, her peals of laughter like bells. “Return when you promised, Deliverer. Or I’ll come and bring you back myself.” He nods to Tribios. “Be safe, both of you.”

“Bye, De!” Tribios links her arm with Phainon’s. She waves. “See you tomorrow!”

Phainon cups his mouth. “See you tomorrow, Mydei! I love you!” he shouts, unabashed and grinning brighter than the bridge to the stars.

The crowd swoons. Mydei doesn’t notice them. His attention is fixed on Phainon, caped in luminous starry white. Kremnos’ braids in his hair. Armored and adorned in Okheman ruby and gold, bearing sigils marked by each Chrysos Heir. Beautiful, and maddening. Unshaken.

Mydei’s smile hurts with pride. He lifts a hand. Phainon’s words wrap around him like armor, like a blanket, like an embrace. He’ll say them back when his husband returns victorious, and more.

You too. I’ll be waiting.

A flash of bright light, like lightning in the distance. Then Phainon and Tribios are gone. Dust kicks up in the absence of the Eschatheion.

And now, Mydei thinks as he faces hundreds of emotional citizens with teleslates poised and an honor guard that only reddens more when he tries to catch their eyes—he has his own battle to fight.

Krateros doesn’t laugh, but it’s the closest Mydei has ever seen him do so.

“The Okhemas gave you a hard time?” He hedges, falling into step beside Mydei as they walk toward the detachment’s part of the city.

Mydei shakes his head, exhausted. “It wasn’t just Okhemans. More than a quarter of them were our people. One of them tried to pat me and said Phainon would be back soon.” He pinches the bridge of his nose. “I know he’ll be back soon. They’re more worked up than I am.”

Krateros grunts. “I do not blame them. An army that lets one of its generals walk into the enemy’s camp is not fit to conquer even the smallest village.”

Mydei’s knee-jerk instinct is to protest. To wage war on the Cosmos is a death knell for Amphoreus, no matter how strong the Heirs may be. Phainon didn’t endure millions of cycles to spearhead cosmic warfare, quite the opposite, and the mantle of military leadership is the last thing Mydei wants for his husband.

But Mydei’s tired beyond words, of which he would need many to debate with his teacher. It is Krateros’ way, the old and true Kremnoan way, to think in terms of strategy and battle and troops. It is also Mydei’s way, but not his only one. Securing the future of Amphoreus will need many different approaches; the Heirs’ compromise with the Station being case in point.

“The Station is not our enemy. We need their help, and they need our cooperation,” Mydei reminds him. “It’s a partnership that suits us for the time being.”

“Until Lord Phainon’s condition stabilizes, I assume?”

Krateros’ tone is odd. Not hesitant, but a shade of it. Mydei glances at him. His teacher’s face gives nothing away.

“Yes,” Mydei acquieses. “Until Phainon is better.”

Krateros is quiet as they stroll. They’re nearly past the Marmoreal Palace when he says, “It’s time to officially announce it to our people, then.”

“Announce what?” Mydei asks absently, noticing multiple clusters of people in and around the baths. Animated debates, by the looks of it.

“Lord Phainon’s condition?” Krateros sounds confused.

Mydei frowns, facing him. “The people know of it, Teacher. It’s obvious.” They have made no effort to hide Phainon’s rhimágmata since the beginning.

Krateros crosses his arms disapprovingly. “We should not wait until Lord Phainon is showing. Our people should hear it from the mouth of their regent, not from whispers on the streets or those silly teleslates. A royal pregnancy is no small matter, Mydeimos.”

Mydei stumbles. Krateros catches his shoulder.

“A royal—a royal what?” Mydei exclaims.

They stare at each other, equally stupified.

“You said—” Krateros says, voice cracking.

“I know what I said but—” Mydei says, high-pitched.

“You just confirmed it—”

“That’s not what I meant—”

Severely, Krateros interjects, “I know fatherhood is a difficult subject, even more so for our people and yourself, but you should honor your consort and proclaim the new heir to the people—”

“There is no heir, Phainon is—”

“—the inheritor of the Worldbearer’s divinity, and hence best suited to bear a child of miracles!” someone shouts from the baths. It echoes through the hall, followed by a cacophony of voices, thumps of fists, and clatters of goblets on marble and stone.

The world stops, flips over, and punches Mydei square in the chest. The next thing he knows, he’s pushing through the crowds, panic and Krateros close at his heels. He has to find the source, has to know the full context of that sentence.

In the middle of the Bath of Plenty, nearly a hundred people form a circle. Several figures stand in the middle, huffing and puffing as if having run a marathon.

A woman gowned in the Grove’s colors glares at a man with gold foil in his long hair. She announces, sharp and cutting, “Approaching this from the angle of divinity is short-sighted. Interpretations of the Titans’ divine powers have fluctuated every Era. Just because Lord Phainon is a demigod doesn’t mean he can somehow defy basic anatomy and conceive a child. He is still a man.”

The long-haired man crosses his arms. “I would have thought a scholar of the Grove to not be so close-minded. Lord Phainon is not merely a man. He is a Chrysos Heir and the Deliverer of the Dawn. Within him is the divinity of Kephale, the Father of Creation. What other authority can grant exceptions to our mortal rules?”

The Grove scholar scoffs. “Where does it say in any of the theological scriptures that Kephale can permit pregnancy in the male form?”

“Once again,” the long-haired man says, enunciating each syllable, “you are so fixated on Lord Phainon’s male form that you are blinded to the greater implications of his demigod status—”

“Blinded?” the Grove scholar repeats, hands curling into fists.

Quickly, a woman with a purple sash decorated with butterflies steps forward. “Why are we still debating the possibility of conception when there’s already more than enough evidence that the Deliverer is carrying?”

A roar of reactions fills the baths. Disbelieving gasps, loud cheers; someone says from the upper balcony: “Hear, hear.”

The long-haired man raises his hands, backtracking. “I believe that’s a bit too hasty a conjecture at this point in time.”

“The signs are quite clear,” the woman continues fervently, waving her hands. “Glowing skin. Looser robes. Needing to be carried by his lord husband to their rooms, even!”

There are multiple rounds of dreamy sighs.

The Grove scholar pointedly says, “That theory has even less evidence than Lord Phainon being able to grow a womb.”

Another voice chimes in from the edge of the circle: “Who are we to say Lord Phainon requires a womb? The Father of Creation birthed humanity through breath alone—”

“Are we to put such stock in myth and metaphor—” the Grove scholar snaps, but someone else from a gaggle of pink-robed librarians thrusts a scroll midair.

“Whether or not Lord Phainon possessed a womb before is immaterial!” the new participant declares confidently. “Based on this book that the heroes from beyond the sky gifted us, it is entirely probable that divinity can awaken latent instincts beyond the prescribed abilities of the demigods—changing things like their natural scents and even genitalia to accommodate a pregnancy!”

Several people raise their goblets in enthusiastic toast, while others cringe and shake their heads. More and more citizens join the circle. Some are wrapped in towels, others half-dressed in bath robes. Wine and water slosh onto the floors.

A woman near the fountain calls out, sounding frustrated, “Shouldn’t we be celebrating the possibility instead of interrogating it? Era Nova is now upon us, thanks to the Chrysos Heirs and their comrades. If Lord Phainon truly carries a child, it is a blessed one. Let us honor it!”

A voice barks from atop a bench, “You want to celebrate a rumor? Do you not think that Lord Phainon and his husband would have announced such a momentous occasion were it true? Why are all of you so eager to hasten falsehoods?”

A man insists over the din, “I heard from my second cousin’s wife’s nephew-in-law that his neighbor saw Lord Mydeimos purchasing a basket of conception medicine yesterday morning!”

“You fool,” another man says from the opposite side. “What kind of source reliability is that? I was actually there at Marmoreal Market yesterday. The Prince was just buying vegetables and fruits from Demetria—”

“Who buys cremni pear if not for pregnancy?” the first man demands.

“Cremni pear can be used for any muscle ache, you oaf—”

“Who are you calling an oaf!”

The two lunge at each other and wrestle in the shallows of the pool. They’re swallowed up by the crowd.

“Why are we putting all the burden of proof on Lord Phainon?” drawls a young woman lounging on a kline. “Last time I checked, it takes at least two people to make a child. Lord Phainon’s obviously able to bear one, with those hips of his, but why are we not questioning the position of Lord Mydeimos? No offense, but maybe he’s the infertile one.”

Brief, sparse mutterings of agreement are instantly drowned out by a tide of angry shouts.

“Take that back!” A Kremnoan wades toward the young woman, looking furious. “Prince Mydeimos is Lord Phainon’s lawful husband. He is the embodiment of Strife who stood alone against the black tide—you think someone like him can’t sire a child?”

“Perhaps that time alone with the black tide rendered his seed moot—”

“Are you calling our Prince impotent?!”

There are slaps and shoves. A sandal flies across the room. It hits someone else entirely. Numerous scuffles break out.

“Blasphemy!”

“Prudence!”

“Preposterous!”

“Lord Phainon deserves peace, not prodding!” a bath attendant yells, hoisting a bath bucket defensively.

“So we should just ignore the biggest miracle since Era Nova?” another snaps, wielding a pair of soapstones. “He’s not just anyone! If he’s with child, Okhema should rejoice!”

Two muscular bathers stand chest to chest, veins bulging. The taller one says, “If Lord Phainon carries the heir to your kingdom, why did your prince let him go beyond the sky when he should be resting in confinement?”

The other bather sneers. “We do not treat our mothers like delicate flowers. Lord Phainon is the Crown Prince’s only equal. He alone is strong enough to carry the blessed heir and carry out his mission beyond the sky. And unlike others, we have full trust in our prince-consort’s capabilities—”

He’s tackled into the water. The baths reverberate with yells, swearing, more splashing. An entire fruit platter is hurled like a discus across the pool. It hits the pink-robed scholars with a wet splat, triggering another brawl.

The Grove scholar tries to shout over the chaos, “Order! Calm yourselves and be rational!”

She’s promptly jostled aside by a wide-eyed man with his hands folded in prayer. He chants over and over, “The star signs did not lie, the star signs did not lie, I knew it the moment I saw that constellation!”

“Lord Mydei,” Castorice says.

Mydei jolts out of his stupor. Castorice hovers over him, wringing her hands. He’s sitting on a kline with a goblet of juice in one hand. He downs it in one gulp. His head spins, full of cotton. His heart is pounding hard. Behind Castorice, Krateros is alternating between watching the debacle and scrutinizing him.

“Cas,” Mydei rasps when he finds his voice, “I think the city’s gone mad.”

She gives him a wan smile. “Come, let’s get you to your rooms. It’s getting much too wild here.”

Mydei numbly lets her and Krateros guide him back to the Heirs’ apartments. It’s not until he’s slumped over on the floor of his and Phainon’s room with the chimeras sniffing at him that he’s able to think coherently again.

Krateros stands in the hallway, looking pensive. He mutters something to Castorice. She nods and quietly closes the door before joining Mydei on the floor.

They say nothing for a few minutes. Beagle Coconut starts to make biscuits on Mydei’s lap. Honey Fruitcake perches in the crook of Castorice’s elbow and watches his mate contentedly. Mydei, in a rare moment of weakness, flops onto his back, holding Beagle Coconut so he doesn’t startle. Castorice does the same.

Mydei musters himself and says to the ceiling, “Cas?”

“Hmm?”

“Why are the people debating about Phainon having—Phainon being able to—” The words traitorously clog up in his throat.

Castorice says, very softly, “To get pregnant?”

Mydei makes a strangled noise. “Yes,” he chokes. “That.”

Castorice reaches out and, after a brief second of hesitation, lays a gentle hand on his wrist. Her skin is cooler than Mydei’s, but comforting. She replies, “The Titan of Worldbearing has always been a heated topic of debate.”

“Has,” Mydei swallows. “Has the debate always focused on that part, though?”

Castorice is quiet, then, “It’s become more popular, recently.”

Mydei stares at the ceiling.

“Lord Mydei?”

“Just Mydei, Cas.”

“Mydei,” Castorice says. “Are you angry? That people are talking about it?”

Is he? Is anger the feeling that tingles at the base of his spine when he thinks of Phainon and pregnancy in the same sentence, or a different sort of madness? Is it fury at a perceived insult that makes his jaw clench every time someone speaks of Phainon conceiving, Phainon carrying—or something else entirely?

“No,” Mydei says. “I’m not angry.”

“Oh.” He can feel the relief radiating from Castorice. “That’s good to hear.”

He thinks about yesterday, and today, and feels a little raw. “Cas, the thing that made me crystallize Marmoreal Market.”

“I heard,” she says not unkindly. “Stelle and Caelus are many things, but they are not subtle.” She pauses. “I—I suppose I wasn’t subtle as well, when the topic was brought up in the baths a few days ago.”

“Is that why you were in the baths today? Because of the debate?”

Castorice admits meekly, “I wanted to hear the other theories.”

Tension drains out of him. He sighs. “So… last time, did Caelus really almost get into a fight?”

Castorice laughs, light as a butterfly’s wing. “Yes. Dan Heng smiled a lot that day.”

“I can imagine.” Lucky man. Phainon in full righteous anger is quite a treat himself, but Mydei hasn’t seen him like that since the first Council meeting after the First Dawn. Perhaps they should join another one later this week.

Beagle Coconut falls asleep on Mydei. Honey Fruitcake slips from Castorice’s arm,  waddles over Mydei, and hops on his belly to curl protectively around his mate. Mydei huffs but lays a hand over them both.

They ponder the ceiling in comfortable silence. His heart no longer feels like it’s about to break out between his ribs when his teleslate buzzes, followed by Castorice’s.

“I’ll take care of it,” Castorice says, already thumbing a response.

“How bad is it?”

Castorice reads her teleslate. “Not bad, actually. Lady Aglaea and Hyacine sorted out the baths. Cifera mentioned some acolytes who followed Zagreus may have gotten to the wine.” She raises a brow at something Cipher must have typed. “She neither claims nor denies involvement. She does say your and Lord Phainon’s moment at the Eschatheion helped.”

“She saw us?”

“Both of you are on the front page of the news.” Castorice shows him the screen. His and Phainon’s embrace is on full colored display, complete with the crowd cheering in the background.

It’s a photoslate that will absolutely circulate throughout Amphoreus within the day, if not the hour. Underneath are comments from countless citizens, which continue for several hundred pages. Mydei’s eyes glaze over just thinking about reading them, but a quick scan over the first page tells him enough.

“Mydei?” Castorice touches his arm. “Are you okay?”

“Most of them are quite convinced,” he says, “about Phainon being able to, uh.”

“Get pregnant?” Castorice supplies helpfully, reading from the comments. “Bear the world? Bring a new dawn?”

“Do you think he can?” Mydei blurts out.

Castorice’s gaze falls to her lap. “Perhaps the only one who can answer that is Phainon himself.” She takes a deep breath and meets Mydei’s eyes. “But I think what’s more important is, how do you feel about that? Whether or not he’s able to?”

To think about it is a struggle in itself. A churn of odd shame and inexplicable want burns under his skin. His whole body trembles, alight with something brighter and fiercer than any Coreflame.

Castorice picks up on it. Her expression softens. “You don’t have to have the answer now. Take some time and think about it.” She smoothes out her skirt and stands. “I’ll be visiting the dromases today. Would you like to join me?”

Mydei, for lack of anything else and in desperate need for company, can only agree. He deposits the chimeras on the kline, freshens up, and lets Castorice take the lead for the day.

They visit the dromases; Mydei gives Kokopo the Third a thorough cleaning, partly to give his hands something to do. Castorice somehow manages to maneuver the dromases to stand around them, blocking Mydei from inquisitive onlookers.

Lunch is taken picnic-style with Hyacine in the Garden of Life. Mydei freezes when Aglaea glides onto the sunlit pavilion, but she simply tops off his juice and finishes half of the tiropitakias, famished. Hyacine falls asleep midway, stretched out on the grass, exhausted from the surge of injuries from the baths.

“Rest,” Aglaea tells him, reclining on the blanket. “I believe we shall all need it in the coming days.”

“What does that mean,” Mydei wants to ask out of reflex. He decides not to, choosing to preserve the delicate peace. He joins them on the cool soft grass and closes his eyes.

The day passes in a similar fashion, attending to other matters around Okhema. Surveying the rebuilding of the Path of Parting. Looking over the archives of the detachment’s makeshift library. Organizing the newest batch of chimeras into their work teams.

Castorice accompanies Mydei the whole time. He suspects she purposefully planned places to go where the citizens can’t easily follow them. He’s grateful for her. But from the way Cipher keeps spamming Mydei’s private messages, she and Castorice seem to have something planned for the evening.

“It’s no trouble at all,” Castorice keeps insisting as they walk the hallway to Mydei and Phainon’s rooms. “Come join us for dinner. We’ll take a stroll around Okhema. Perhaps we can stargaze later tonight.”

“I might take a walk,” Mydei teases. “You might gaze at something else entirely.”

“Mydei!” She covers her face. “It’s not like that!”

“Don’t let me keep you,” he urges. “I’ll be fine. I have to take care of the chimeras anyway.”

Castorice peeks at him through her fingers. “You’re sure?”

“I’m sure,” Mydei says solemnly. “You deserve this, too. Go enjoy yourself.”

Castorice’s cheeks are tinged a light pink as she bids Mydei farewell. Mydei watches her leave before sending a conciliatory message to Cipher and going inside.

“I’m home,” he says to Beagle Coconut and Honey Fruitcake. They crowd his feet, awoo-ing insistently. “Hungry?”

He fixes the chimeras' dinner and watches them eat, not having much of an appetite himself. The sun is starting to set, filling the room with honey-golden light. It’s the kind of view he and Phainon would watch from the balcony, a platter of fine cheeses and fresh fruits balanced between them as they spoke about everything, and sometimes nothing.

He steps onto the balcony. It welcomes him with a sky awash with rose and gold. But it doesn’t feel the same. Not like when it hugs the curve of Phainon’s cheek, catching on a smile meant only for his husband—holding it there, as if time couldn’t bear to let go.

Strife. Feeling somewhat forlorn and foolish because of it, Mydei checks his teleslate. No new messages from Phainon. It’s normal. Communication between Amphoreus and the Station is unreliable at best. It’s also not late enough in the day that Phainon or Tribios would return to the Express, where Phainon would call Mydei.

Mydei closes the inbox and spots the photoslate from earlier. His finger hovers over it. He can’t help but think back to his conversation with Castorice, replaying each moment in slow detail.

He ruled out having children long before he met Phainon. The weight of his lineage and the dark, overglossed custom of patricide in Castrum Kremnos had made the idea unbearable. He refused to subject any child to the weight he once carried, or be forced to do what he’d done to Eurypon.

But here in Okhema, he’s grown fond of little ones running afoot, the sound of their laughter ringing in the streets, the halls. He watched Kremnoan children grow up in the Holy City, unburdened by the expectation of martyrdom in Nikador’s name. Ending the dynasty had not doomed them. It had been its own kind of mercy, giving them a new beginning.

Phainon, he knows, grew up with many children around Aedes Elysiae. He lost them too, countless times across countless cycles. But the grief hadn’t stopped him from letting the city’s children swing from his arms, or dragging him into games during patrol breaks. He laughs at their jokes and listens to their stories. He kneels when they run to him.

Yet they’ve never spoken of adopting or having any of their own. Era Nova brought with it a new set of challenges, far-reaching and far more complex than they had imagined. Their duties as Chrysos Heirs had not ended with the First Dawn.

Mydei’s eyes fall back to the photoslate.

Whatever flicker of embarrassment he might have felt is eclipsed by something deeper, more powerful. An ache that takes his breath away.

He has seen his husband in rage, in sorrow, in unspeakable grief. He’s also seen him in laughter, in luminous joy, decadently in love and unashamed of it in Mydei’s arms.

In the photoslate, with their bodies fitted together like puzzle pieces, Phainon glows. The one who bears the world, at peace.

Would he still glow, cradling a child with Mydei’s smile and his own blue eyes? What would he look like, carrying another—who might inherit Mydei’s nose and Phainon’s hair, a tiny echo of them both? Would Phainon be as content with a third? A fourth? Would he be at peace in a home filled with ruckus laughter, and little hands reaching up to them both?

Mydei’s heart could be in tatters, for the way longing carves through it.

Oh, he thinks. Then, I have to talk to Phainon.

Beloved

Praise the sun!

Mydei, I know it’s later than usual, but we’re back on the Express. You might be asleep already, so I’ll call you tomorrow.

So much happened today at the Station, a lot of it quite strange. Madam Herta’s line of questioning was completely different than before. She seemed more… caring? Maybe that’s not the word. Perhaps cautious?

The crew has also been hovering more so than usual. Sunday in particular has stuck to my side. He said something about “warding off disharmonious energies” which I thought was kind of him.

I’ll tell you the whole of it in the morning. For now, goodnight and rest easy.

I miss you already, my lion.

Anaxagoras

Then let me ask you

Crown Prince,

Perhaps there is still something more I can teach you.

I expect you at the Grove tomorrow, at the start of Lucid Hour.

We will speak—uninterrupted.

Chapter End Notes

Fun fact: crystal lizard satay is a real in-game consumable! It recovers 4 Technique Points, but each team member loses 15% of their Max HP. Did Caelus and Stelle know that beforehand? Probably not, with their iron stomachs.

On an unrelated note, I, too, would participate in a baths brawl over Mydei and Phainon and their potential future cosmic babies.
