Chapter Summary

The air leaves Mydei’s lungs. He stares at Anaxa’s back. Anaxa looks over his shoulder with an arched brow. “So shocked, Crown Prince. Is that not why we are here?”

“You believe it to be possible?” Mydei asks, voice tremulous despite himself.

“Which part? That Phainon can bear children or that you want so ardently for him to do so?”

Chapter Notes

Apologies for the late update! I moved, got sick (still sick), and had a few major life changes… thanks again for so many lovely comments and the support!

No beta, and all of this was edited on mobile, so please pardon any formatting or other errors.

Mydei does not know what to expect when he steps down from the Space Anchor.

Perhaps a legion of loyal Nousporists ready to march him to the Luminary Throne. Maybe one of Anaxa’s contraptions, ready to spring on him in the name of field trial experimentation. Or even the Sage himself, waiting patiently with his gun aimed at Mydei’s crotch.

Given Anaxa’s taste for the theatrics, Mydei would not have been surprised if the man has gone out of his way to make answering his summons as difficult as possible. Especially when today’s meeting undoubtedly concerns Phainon.

For a man who claims the position of teacher alone, Anaxa plays the role of father far too convincingly.

But perhaps Mydei is being overly imaginative, and rather unfair to Anaxa. Exhaustion gnaws at him down to the bone. A night tossing and turning and ruminating over yesterday’s revelations has left him drained in a way fighting titankin never had. Rest had eluded him and thus his brain has, on the worst possible day, turned into mush.

So when he arrives at the Grove, the sight of Stelle sitting criss-crossed on a bench at the head of the Woven Path, serenely braiding three strands of long grass, is enough to make him stop in his tracks and briefly doubt his own eyes.

Stelle brightens up upon seeing him, tucking the braided grass into her pocket. She waves enthusiastically. “Hi Mydei!”

This shameless woman. Does she have any idea of the domino effect she and her brother have started? He rounds on her with a newfound surge of energy. “Trailblazer—”

Stelle yelps, scrambling off the bench. “Mercy, Mydei! I come in peace!”

“I hope you come bearing an explanation,” Mydei thunders, “and twenty-five thousand balance coins.”

Stelle pauses, one foot hovering in the air. “Only twenty-five?”

“Phainon will get the other twenty-five out of Caelus. Now get back over here.”

Stelle squeaks and hops out of range of his gauntlets. “Five minutes is all I ask! Mydei!” she whines with the same intonation Phainon uses.

Unfortunately for her, the rendition lacks the big blue puppy eyes that make it work. Mydei crosses his arms, schooling his face into stone. “Speak.”

“Okay, so in the beginning—” Stelle stops, frowning. “Actually, I might need more than five minutes, unless you want the super abridged version.”

“What manner of explanation,” Mydei says, “could possibly necessitate an abridged version?”

Stelle seems to think very deeply. She counts something on her fingers, then draws some nonsensical shapes in the air. After a few seconds of this, she says, “So do you remember how in Cycle Zero—”

“I no longer wish to know,” Mydei groans, palming the tension behind the bridge of his brows.

“This time though was because of a book about Kephale,” Stelle rolls over his protest, tiptoeing closer once she figures Mydei won’t yank her into a headlock. “We found it during the clean-up here. Dan Heng needed help translating it, so we asked some other scholars and, well…”

“The rest is history?” Mydei has a good idea now which parts of the book needed help translating.

She grins, the tiniest hint of mischief afoot. “History to be made?”

The base of his spine tingles. Strife makes its approval known as his thymós stirs under his skin, tattoos crackling scarlet. Stelle’s grin widens knowingly.

“That audacity will be your downfall,” Mydei grumbles. He bumps their shoulders lightly to soften the words. “Why are you here? I’d have thought you’d do everything in your power to avoid me, considering how fast you and Caelus fled Okhema.”

Stelle winces. “Anaxa mentioned you were coming. I wanted to come and say hi.” She rubs the back of her head. “I also wanted to apologize. Cas told me you might have had a rough day yesterday.”

Mydei shakes his head. “Keep your apologies and keep me company instead.” He starts up the Woven Path. “Though I warn you, I can’t guarantee your safety if you’re in my vicinity once Anaxagoras catches sight of me.”

Stelle falls in step beside him. Mydei extends his arm, which she takes with a happy squeal. “I don’t think he’s that mad.” At Mydei’s doubtful side-eye, she adds, “I mean it! He said a lot of really complicated words and made some things blow up yesterday in his lab, but he seemed fine this morning.”

Fantastic. Maybe Anaxa had expended enough energy to let Mydei crawl from the Grove mostly intact. Or maybe that’s wishful thinking. He says, “Anaxagoras could be splitting his soul into a dozen fragments and still say he’s fine.” Which he has, multiple times across many cycles.

“But better fine than not, right?” Stelle needles. “Speaking of, how are you doing? With everything that’s happened? I heard about the debate in the baths.”

“Debate is one way to put it. Castorice told you?”

Her eyes dart away. “Not just her.”

“Nevermind,” Mydei sighs. “I won’t be surprised if news of it has reached every corner of Amphoreus. Don’t let it weigh on you,” he says when Stelle looks at the ground guiltily. “I had time to think about it. I’m fine.”

She peeks at him. “Truly?

With heavy, weary eyes, Mydei looks to the sky. The sun is overcast by a smattering of puffy white clouds. If he was a more imaginative man, he might imagine Phainon looking his way, too. Might see the imperfect, crooked smile Phainon reserves just for him.

Urgency curls around quiet longing. It’s the feeling that’s kept him up all night, staring at the ceiling and seriously considering taking the Eschatheion to fetch Phainon from the Station himself. To see his face again. To know he’s safe. To sit him down and tell him the truth of the matter, and hear what he has to say.

“I will be, once I speak to Phainon about it,” Mydei tells Stelle.

She has a sort of bug-eyed look. Mydei attempts to lighten the mood. “If you were anticipating a… what do you and Caelus call it? A crashout? You are a bit late.”

“Who, how,” Stelle sputters. “Cas?”

“Not just her,” Mydei says, tugging her along, satisfied with the utter astonishment on her face. “There won’t be a repeat performance, by the way. You’ll have to get the full details on your own.”

“Mydei!” Stelle squawks before hurrying to keep up. “Hey slow down, each of your steps are two of mine, you know. Oi, Mydei!”

He takes the lead in crossing the bridges that connect the Grove’s rebuilt grounds. Classes must be in session, as there are no scholars outside. Construction tents have been set up along the way with teams of people from different city-states pouring over floor plans and drawings.

The Grove was among the few city-states unanimously voted for priority reconstruction, both out of respect and necessity. Remnants of the black tide still linger, and the unknown Cosmos hover above in the place of Aquila's threatening power.

Erudition has borne great fruits in Amphoreus. The Grove, its newly restored plethora of scholars and wealth of knowledge, remains one of their greatest strengths.

Mydei greets the reconstruction teams with a nod and a wave, which are returned enthusiastically. “How goes the recovery?” he asks Stelle as they pass the Serene Court of Learning.

Compared to the wreckage that the first days of Era Nova left behind, the change is striking. Stone walkways lie restored and swept clean. Grass has begun to regrow in wide patches. New pillars lift skyward with budding vines curling around the bases.

Stelle, who has so far been glancing at him like one might study a particularly colorful insect, startles and replies, “Ahead of schedule. Most of the Space Anchors are in place and the scholars’ dormitories are finished. We’re going to start bringing in the first batch of books into the Library of Philia today.”

“Oh?” Mydei says mildly. “Is the worldbearing book among them?”

Stelle’s grip tightens in shock as she wails, “Don’t call it that! It sounds so weird coming from you!”

“Is it not, as you and others have declared before, a book about Kephale? Who was the Worldbearing Titan?” He tilts his head, recalling the numerous arguments mentioned in the baths. “The Titan whose coreflame burns inside Phainon who is also called the Deliverer—”

“It’s too cringe in your voice,” Stelle cries. She’s the one to yank Mydei now, marching toward the Dome of Devotion. “Please hurry and get things cleared up with Anaxa so we can go treasure hunting and never talk about this again.”

Mydei snorts, letting himself be pulled inside the Dome. A cool air washes over him, sweet-smelling and fresh. Golden butterflies flutter around them, drawn to their chatter. One lands on Mydei’s gauntlet. Its glow is the same shade as Phainon’s eyes when Mydei first saw him at the new dawn of their world.

“They came back a few days ago,” Stelle says, beaming as a butterfly lands on her outstretched hand. They temper the sound of their footsteps, the volume of their voices. This is still, even after being ravaged by Destruction, a place for contemplation and reverence. “Not as many as before,” Stelle says, “but more than what we were expecting.”

Mydei hums, watching the golden butterflies leave faint traces of light in their paths. Much had been lost in the battle for Amphoreus, losses that Era Nova couldn’t wholly restore. A wealth of soul essence had bled away when they broke through the false sky.

By the time they catalogued the damage, most of the Creation Nymphs were gone.

“They’ll grow in number,” Mydei assures, letting his butterfly fly off before nudging Stelle’s arm. “It might take some time, but the next generation that follows will be free of their original code.”

She sniffles, swipes a hand across her nose, and nods fiercely. “Right! They don’t have to worry about being used as Irontomb’s data. They can just be butterflies and beetles and whatever else they want to be.” She coos to the butterfly on her hand, “Don’t worry, little one. We’ll never let you be part of that awful system ever again. I promise!”

Mydei smiles. That’s the spirit, Trailblazer. For all the headaches that Stelle and Caelus give him, shameless as they can be, they are the Heirs’ greatest friends and supporters. The new silver tracks glittering in the stars beyond the sky are proof of that.

With renewed vigor, Stelle marches them up the slope leading to the Luminary Throne. When they’re a few paces away, she turns to Mydei. “Ready?” she asks, disentangling their arms but holding onto his wrist.

Mydei takes in the entrance to the highest point of the Grove, outlined in moss and stone. A breeze floats down to them, bringing with it the faint smell of parchment and metal and herbs.

The Luminary Throne was never meant for a laboratory. Too sacred, the devout murmured, bowing their heads as they prayed. Too storied, noted the more cautious, wary of staking claim where a Titan’s Coreflame once slumbered. Too remote, a few confessed, for at such heights the stars provided closer company than people.

It only suited Anaxagoras to take those as recommendations, not warnings.

“Mydei?” Stelle murmurs with a squeeze of his wrist. Her eyes are solemn, focused, darting over his face as if trying to find something. “Want me to come with you? I can just stand to the side for moral support. I won’t even make a peep.”

Mydei chuckles. “Anaxa said he and I will speak uninterrupted. We both know he means for us to be alone.”

He wonders briefly if it was the salaciousness of the rumors, or the possibility of them having some kernel of truth, that prompted such a message from Anaxa. Theirs has always been a cordial relationship strengthened by a love for learning and an appreciation for dromases. He can only hope he hasn’t lost that mutual respect.

Stelle nods slowly and lets go. “I’ll wait here then.”

“Still want to see the show?”

She shakes her head and reaches inside her jacket, pulling out the grass braid. Upon closer inspection, Mydei realizes she’s made it in the Kremnoan style using both orange and blue-green stalks of grass. Messy and uneven, but complete. “Think of it as being there for my friends,” Stelle says, pressing the braid into his hand. “I’ve been practicing, see?”

Mydei smiles. “I see.” He pats her head. “It’s a worthy effort.”

Stelle grins. “Good luck, Mydei. See you on the other side.”

He can feel her gaze on his back as he ascends the last few steps to the Luminary Throne. The grass braid is a comforting weight in his pocket. The mossy walls around him give way to loamy earth, to thick branches that eventually part and reveal glimpses of clouds.

When he reaches the top, the sky above is somehow dark and star-studded. It hadn’t even been a half a quint since he arrived. It should be around Lucid Hour. Mydei blinks, bewildered.

Then he spots Anaxagoras. The Sage’s lithe form cuts a sharp picture where the Luminary Throne once stood, stark amidst stacks of books and tables of cauldrons.

Anaxagoras turns. His gun rests comfortably in its holster at his hip. Even from this distance, the metal on the handle gleams, freshly polished. Around them, gentle sifts of dusty light flow like currents, cosmic and almost arcane.

“Crown Prince,” Anaxa greets. His voice, velvety and almost lyrical, warps through the space like a command.

“Anaxagoras—”

A bullet slashes past Mydei’s cheek, barely missing him. Behind him, a stone pillar shatters. Red bleeds from Anaxa’s eye and blurs into a streak as he takes position and aims again, his lips set in a neutral line.

So this is how it will be. Mydei accepts the challenge with solemn determination, as he has all challenges before.

The clearing ruptures with the ring of bullets, dirt exploding where Mydei stood not a second ago. Mydei dodges and weaves, ducks and spins, his tattoos flashing as his entire body thrums. The rhythm of battle is one that his body knows by heart, though the nature of this fight is a far cry from the norm.

“Anaxagoras,” he calls out.

“Don’t interrupt me,” Anaxa replies coolly, and fires off another round that cuts a jagged line through the air and takes all of Mydei’s concentration to avoid.

Mydei won’t retaliate. There’s a lesson to this, he knows, and he tries to parse it from the patterns of Anaxa’s attacks. The man isn’t aiming to maim, that’s for sure; otherwise Mydei would have been riddled in holes from the moment he stepped onto the hallowed grounds.

Anaxa gives no quarter, not even as he reloads and watches the previous bullets ricochet around Mydei. Mydei’s gauntlets and boots leave deep grooves in the soil. Sweat gathers on his brow, in his palms.

Then, just as quickly as it started, it stops. Anaxa lifts his gun and checks the chamber with lazy nonchalance. Mydei breathes slowly, wiping dirt from his face. He expects Anaxa to reload again and start shooting for real.

Anaxa does not. He nods as if confirming something, holsters the gun, and crosses his arms as he meets Mydei’s eyes. “Your senses are as sharp as ever, Mydeimos,” he says casually, as if he hasn’t emptied entire clips into the floor, the walls.

Mydei straightens up and rasps, “You needed to use your gun to confirm that?”

“Experimentation is the best way to prove or disprove a theory.” Anaxa gestures to the bullet holes and damage around them. “As we’ve so demonstrated.”

“What theory necessitated such an experiment?” Mydei asks, eyeing him.

“Was I not clear enough in my message?”

Mydei says, “You wanted to teach me a lesson. Because of Phainon.” The last part wasn’t mentioned in Anaxa’s summons, but what else could possibly warrant such a display?

“Like I said, your senses remain sharp.” Anaxa turns back to the table, pushing through scrolls and trinkets. “Good. You’ll need that when you and Phainon decide to have children.”

The air leaves Mydei’s lungs. He stares at Anaxa’s back. Anaxa looks over his shoulder with an arched brow. “So shocked, Crown Prince. Is that not why we are here?”

“You believe it to be possible?” Mydei asks, voice tremulous despite himself.

“Which part? That Phainon can bear children or that you want so ardently for him to do so?”

An incredulous huff leaves Mydei at the sheer boldness of this man. “Let’s start with the first, perhaps.”

Anaxa turns and regards him with unsettling calm. There’s a small round object in his hands. “Phainon shattered a space-time dimension and drew an Aeon’s blood when he was nothing more than code. Do you think he is incapable of carrying a child as he is now?”

“You make the alternative sound like the greater impossibility,” Mydei confesses.

“I believe impossibility is not something Phainon concerns himself with,” Anaxa says smoothly.

In that, they are in agreement. Mydei swallows, tamping down his nerves. “Very well. Then the second? Am I so transparent?”

A wry smile plays on Anaxa’s lips. “On your part, yes. But that is to be expected. You are newly wedded to Kephale’s successor. Era Nova is upon us. Is it not part of the natural proclivity of humans in peacetime to sow seed and see it grow?”

Such a clinical, objective analysis. “It is better to raise children in peace than in war,” Mydei agrees. “But on Phainon’s part—I have yet to speak to him about it. The thought hadn’t even occurred to me until recently.” Until a day ago, in fact. How quickly his whole world can change.

Anaxa’s eye glitters. “The idea came to me much sooner, but I didn’t understand it until yesterday.” He twists the round object, a definite click ringing out.

The night sky above ripples. Stars rearrange themselves in sweeping arcs until a pattern emerges—one that dawns on Mydei immediately.

It is his and Phainon’s constellation. The one that burst into existence when they made love until their divinities resonated with perfect attunement. Sharp lines braided with sinuous curves, as if Kephale and Nikador’s insignias had entwined and quickened into something completely new.

Never has Mydei seen it so close, so clearly rendered outside of the Vortex of Genesis. It can only be seen on moonless nights in Okhema, though he’s always been aware of its presence, constant as sunlight or the brush of an easy breeze.

“Approximately one standard day into Era Nova,” Anaxa says in the cadence of a lecture, “the Express alerted me to the appearance of a new constellation in Amphoreus’ astral system. It had the Station’s scholars in quite a frenzy. The stars that make up a constellation usually have no association with one another, they told me. The patterns we see are simply tricks of perspective. But this one?” Anaxa huffs, and it sounds somewhat impressed. “This one came into existence as one entity. The first of its kind.”

Mydei swallows dryly. He and Phainon had marveled at the sight of it, panting and sated and entangled on a bed of feathers. To him, it had been just a happy coincidence—a timely symbol of their victory, of their reunion, of binding themselves as husbands.

“The Station and other groups tried to lay claim to it,” Anaxa continues, almost scornfully. “Perhaps to study it further, or for the bragging rights of ownership. They chose to not follow through after I visited. A wise choice, in my opinion.”

Mydei searches through his memories, quickly recalling the first and only time Anaxa was requested to go to the Station. “You two came home early. Phainon said you were banned from going back ever again.”

Anaxa waves his hand flippantly. “As if they can stop me. But no matter. I made my point clear enough.”

“You protected the constellation,” Mydei realizes. “That’s—that matters.”

Anaxa’s piercing look relaxes just enough to reveal the care underneath. “I knew it was connected to you two. What I didn’t know was what it might mean. Until yesterday.”

Mydei puts the pieces together. “The debate?”

“A rather uproarious spectacle,” Anaxa says, sounding oddly similar to Aglaea. “But even such chatter can reveal some fascinating theories. To will the transformation of Worldbearing from an epithet to an ability—now that is something else, indeed. And there is already some evidence to support it.”

Anaxa tips his head back. Mydei follows suit, drinking in the bright lines of the constellation etched across the heavens, as much a mark of defiance as of love. Heat floods his body, his thymós alight in the face of revelation, the implications of it. His and Phainon’s stars sparkle at him, as if in greeting.

“Isn’t it ironic?” Anaxa says at last. “You both have walked the path of Destruction, and yet you are also capable of the miracle of creation.”

Creation. That is what their constellation is. Not just a symbol, not mere coincidence. It is something born into the Cosmos itself. A product of their joining.

Mydei works his jaw. “I thought you didn’t believe in miracles,” he says, wrung out, braced with anticipation.

“I may be known for blasphemy,” Anaxa says, darkly amused, “but miracles?” His lips quirk. “Perhaps what we call a miracle is simply the product of humanity’s outrageous will pushing itself against impossible odds.”

Era Nova. Their survival. Bonds shattered and reforged stronger each cycle. The dawn-drenched mornings, the soft pillowed evenings. Phainon’s braid, clasped in gold, with his divinity entwined with Mydei’s forever. The stars they willed into being simply because they loved each other so.

Anaxa walks closer until they’re shoulder to shoulder. Mydei looks at Anaxa helplessly.

“Do you think—Phainon would want to—”

“That is a question best posed to him,” Anaxa cuts in gently. “One I suspect you will ask once he returns.” His gaze is steady, stern but not unkind. “But are you prepared for the consequences if he says yes?”

Mydei’s reply cracks with a half laugh. “Were you prepared when you defended our constellation and got banned from the Station?”

Anaxa rolls his shoulders. “Naturally. I would do it again with ease. But at the end of the day, it is a constellation.” He pauses, tone sobering. “A child, however—a child of a Lord Ravager and a demigod? That is another matter entirely.”

“Phainon isn’t a Lord Ravager anymore,” Mydei protests.

“By choice alone,” Anaxa counters. “Do you really that would dissuade others? From taking an interest in children born from two beings who’ve held Nanook’s attention? Phainon already draws the eyes of the Cosmos just by existing.”

Mydei stiffens. White-hot rage slices through the fog in his head like a lance, clearing it of any doubts and hesitations. His divine powers cannot rival Phainon’s—none of the Heirs’ can —but clarity sears a vow all the same: no person, no sovereign, no lofty god in the Cosmos will ever lay a finger on his husband and their children.

Their children. Strife. The thought is both blade and balm. He could choke on it—the tidal surge beating against his ribs, murmuring of names to be given and kisses bestowed on tiny starry brows.

“Calm yourself,” Anaxa says. The glow of Mydei’s tattoos spill across his face in fierce scarlet shadows. “You are not alone, Mydei. Should danger come, you and Phainon will have an entire world at your backs.”

Aglaea must already know. Castorice and the Trailblazers, too. Hyacine and Tribios won’t be far behind. Cifera either would have guessed from the start, or will quickly take it in stride once she learns of it. The citizens—surely some of the citizens already know, as well, if their enthusiasm in the baths is of any indication. It’s laughable, how Mydei and Phainon may very well be the last to figure it out.

“Thank you,” Mydei says. “Truly, Anaxagoras. Thank you.”

Anaxa shrugs. He twists the round object again. The star-scattered projection dissolves into a honey-gold morning. Clouds like spun sugar drift across a bright blue blanket. Sunlight beams down on them, warm as a blessing.

“Mydei! Anaxa!” Stelle’s voice echoes from the entrance. She’s jogging over and waving her arms, a smile stretching ear to ear. “Oh thank goodness you’re both in one piece—holy shit what happened to the floor—anyway, Phainon and Tribios are back!”

“Thanks is not necessary,” Anaxa muses. “But appreciated nonetheless. Off with you now. You still have a long day ahead.”

The Vortex of Genesis swirls around Mydei as he steps onto polished stone, only one goal in mind.

“He had a pretty rough time, De,” Tribios had said when Mydei and Stelle greeted her, alone, in Okhema. “Yesterday was weird but this morning… The visit was so different compared to before. He probably needs some time to think.”

“Go,” Stelle urged, pressing a comforting hand to Mydei’s arm. “Go to him.”

Mydei went without hesitation.

Just like most of the loopholes in Amphoreus’ original code, the Vortex of Genesis has been sealed off to all but the Chrysos Heirs and the Trailblazers. It now serves as a place of privacy, a liminal space where galaxies within Amphoreus’ astral system spiral above and around in real time.

Mydei hasn’t been here since he and Phainon exchanged their vows, that very first time.

The circular platform soaks beneath the light of a distant supernova. Stars swim around in a thousand kaleidoscopic colors, and the distant crash of waves against ancient stone reverberates through the endless space.

And there he is.

Phainon, perched on the edge of the platform, back to Mydei. His wings have torn through his robes, arching over the floor in ice-gold against midnight-black. Afterimages of a halo flicker around his head, though its light can’t compare to the burning brilliance of the mark of the sun.

Mydei comes closer, letting his footsteps fall naturally. He can see Phainon flinch before slowly turning. His blue eyes are almost too bright, shaded with a tint of yellow. His rhimágmata courses between shades of red and gold. He looks exhausted and lovely and lost.

Mydei says nothing, though his thymós roars at him to close the distance, to sweep Phainon into a crushing embrace, to soothe and settle him in the circle of Mydei’s arms.

Every ounce of his will struggles to be still, to let Phainon make the first delicate move.

Phainon swallows audibly. Then he slowly extends a hand toward Mydei, the other curled over the edge of the platform as if to brace himself.

And Mydei is sinking to his knees beside him, slipping his arms around Phainon and pulling him close, closer still, until Phainon settles atop him and Mydei buries his face into his neck, nearly crumpling with the familiar scent of olive resin and fire. Equal, husband, you’re home. You’re home.

“Mydei,” Phainon whispers, clinging just as fiercely. His wings sweep across the floor to encase them in a protective cocoon. He tucks Mydei’s head under his chin and presses his nose to the crown of Mydei’s head. He’s so warm. Warmer than usual. “Mydei.”

“You’re back,” Mydei says, like a prayer, like a promise fulfilled. “Though I thought I’d be saying that in our rooms and not on the floor here.”

Phainon laughs, a short and stuffy thing. “I couldn’t make it there in time. Forgive the spontaneity. Should I save the ‘I’m home’ for when we get back?”

“Shut up and come here,” Mydei demands.

“I’m already here!” But Phainon wiggles closer until there’s no place they’re not touching. Like this, Mydei swears he can feel their hearts thump against each other. Phainon’s wings block out the lights and sounds of the Vortex, and it’s them. Just them.

The ache in Mydei’s chest finally, blessedly, relaxes and reaches out to its partner.

Their divinities resonate in tandem. Pressure gives way to freedom—to the rapture of subsumption, of two souls dancing and meeting in the middle, heartbreaking for the distance that once divided them and healing in the very act of being together again.

We could make another constellation, Mydei thinks wildly, and smothers a chuckle in Phainon’s skin at his own absurdity.

“What’s so funny?” Phainon asks, tugging at his braid. “Did I miss the punchline to something?”

“There are so many things you’ve missed,” Mydei says, raw.

“Looks like we both had a time of it,” Phainon says, the words trembling at the end. Mydei catches the break and shifts.

“Wait, don’t move,” Phainon insists, pressing Mydei’s head down when he tries to lift himself.

“Why not? Let me see your face.”

Phainon says thickly, “Nuh-uh, not so fast.”

“Are you crying?”

“No. Your hair got in my nose, that’s all.”

“Let me remedy that.” Mydei nips Phainon’s neck, grazing his teeth over the sensitive skin.

Phainon grunts in surprise, but maintains his hold. “Nice try, but that only worked the first time—Mydei!” he yips when Mydei sinks his teeth into muscle. Phainon’s grip loosens just enough for Mydei to roll them over, to see Phainon’s face in full.

“Rascal,” Phainon accuses. His eyes are glazed with stubbornly unshed tears. A dash of bright pink covers his nose. He sniffles again. “Happy? Now you have to look at me like this. You only have yourself to blame.”

“Ridiculous.” Mydei cups his face, tracing the edges of one rhimágmata under Phainon’s eye. “What is to blame? I only see my husband looking like a puppy that’s been left out in the rain.”

Phainon’s wings flutter, the pinions gliding over Mydei’s back. “Well your husband has had a very long day, so excuse him for not looking his best.”

Mydei scoffs. “Do you think I concern myself with how you look? I’ve kissed you covered in titankin guts and blood with no complaint, so spare me your self-flagellation.”

Phainon glares weakly and hooks his hands over the nape of Mydei’s neck. “You know, this wasn’t the romantic homecoming I imagined.”

“Had you stayed with Tribios in Okhema like you usually do, I would have had no trouble sweeping you off your feet and bringing you back to our rooms for a proper reunion.” Mydei leans down and noses along Phainon’s cheek, basking in his scent, his heat.

Phainon exhales shakily and nuzzles back, albeit slow and tired. His body is a livewire of tension. Divine power hums under his skin, tempered, but still electric.

It’s one of those times, then. Mydei sets his mind. He presses gentle, deliberate touches to Phainon’s face, neck, and collarbones. He kisses the bite he made, laving over the tender mark with his tongue. His hands roam over Phainon’s body, working out the tough knots, just as much soothing his husband as he is himself.

Phainon’s breath hitches, an airy sigh slipping his lips. Gradually, he relaxes, sinking into Mydei’s arms. His brow smoothes out, and his grip on Mydei’s nape gentles as his eyes close. “Mmm. Mydei…”

Mydei shushes him, planting a trail of kisses along his jawline. When he reaches the edge of Phainon's mouth, he stops and waits.

Phainon whines, a familiar, intoxicating sound, and tilts his head to connect their lips. It’s a tender kiss. A sweet little peck, just like the ones he gives Mydei every morning.

A million butterflies couldn’t match the burst of emotion in Mydei’s chest. He tips his chin and pecks back, not deepening the kiss but prolonging it, savoring it. This, too, feels like home. Phainon’s breath warm on his skin. His legs wrapped around Mydei’s hips. A gust of cool, sea-tinged air as his wings unfurl and finally rest, splayed out around him.

Phainon pulls back, smiling. “I’m home,” he says, as sweet as his kisses.

“Welcome home.” Mydei cups the back of his head, combing through loose and wavy hair where Phainon’s twin plaits have come undone. Only one messy braid still remains, secured with the gold clasp. He tugs it lightly. “This wasn’t like this when you left.”

“I didn’t mean for your hard work to go to waste.” Phainon sighs. “It was fine until this morning.”

“During which…”

Phainon groans. “Can we go back to kissing?”

Mydei tugs the braid again. “Come on. Up.”

Phainon whines and grumbles the whole time, but he lets Mydei maneuver them into a sitting position, still in Mydei’s lap with his arms draped over his shoulders.

Mydei squeezes Phainon’s hips and peers up at his face. “Still holding out on me? I thought my Deliverer never backs down from a challenge.”

“Hmph,” Phainon sniffs. His lips scrunch up into a pout. Mydei bites back a grin.

“What’s this—a sulk? Has my husband been so bested by a bad morning that he can’t tell me what troubles him?”

“Nothing bested me,” Phainon says immediately. “I held my own at the Station. Tribios can vouch for me!”

“You make it sound like you were in a fight,” Mydei says. “What happened to just meeting with Madam Herta? You mentioned in your message that strange things happened during the visit.”

Phainon nods vigorously. “That’s the thing! When Tribios and I got to the Express yesterday, the crew was already there. Usually, it’s Himeko or Welt who receives us, but everyone was there—even Pom-Pom! Did you know Pom-Pom scolded me for not taking care of myself enough? What did they even mean by that?”

“Breathe,” Mydei reminds him, logging every detail.

Phainon does rather impatiently and carries on. “Then Welt said all of them would be coming with us to the Station, and Sunday would be accompanying me in the visit to ward off disharmonious energies.”

It’s how Phainon mentioned it before. “What did he mean by that?”

“Who knows,” Phainon says, waving his hands. “Maybe remnants of Era Nova’s backlash? Anyway, when we got to the Station, almost a hundred of their scholars were waiting for us. Caelus distracted them, and Sunday got us to Madam Herta.”

Mydei tenses. After the first and only disastrous attempt to study their powers and responses in the Simulated Universe, both sides compromised to keep academic inquiries more akin to personal interviews. Herta’s line of questioning followed a standard script for almost every Heir. For the sake of civility as well as safety.

“When I met with Madam Herta,” Phainon stops. He looks down, eyes lidded. In a move that makes Mydei’s heart trip over itself, Phainon moves his hands to cup his lower belly.

“She kept looking here, and asking if there was anything different with my body since last time,” Phainon says. “Any patterns I’ve noticed. Fatigue, nausea, changes with my appetite or sleep.”

Mydei can’t stop himself. “What did you say?”

Phainon gives a little laugh. “It sounds odd, but I asked if she thought I was pregnant.” He smiles crookedly at Mydei. “Those are the usual symptoms. But I was just joking. It’s plain silly, right?”

He makes it sound so simple. So unaffected. Mydei stares up at him, flummoxed. He should say something. Should chuckle or scoff at such supposed nonsense.

But he knows better. Knows more. Wants more.

At each passing second, Phainon’s cheer fades, replaced by a stunned expression.

“Mydei?” he says, almost disbelieving, starting to squirm on Mydei’s lap. “You don’t… there’s no way you think I’m preg—”

It’s too much. Mydei pins him down with firm hands and says, low and urgent, “Listen—the people think you can bear a child.”

Phainon blinks at him. Mydei waits for him to sputter, to laugh. To refute him and call the very notion ridiculous, and launch into an hours-long exposition on the sheer absurdity of such a statement.

His husband does none of that.

“Oh,” Phainon says instead. His hands have stilled over his abdomen.

“It’s a long story,” Mydei starts, rubbing Phainon’s back as he quickly tries to explain, “Stelle and Cas found a book and they needed help translating it, but it led into a whole debate in the baths and—”

“Do you think I can?” Phainon interrupts, barely louder than a whisper.

Mydei chokes. “What?”

Time stretches. Phainon’s throat works. His gaze flickers with countless unreadable thoughts. “Do you think I can bear a child?”

Mydei’s words crumble in his mouth. His heart pounds, riotous. Phainon slowly leans in. He takes Mydei’s limp hands and places them on his belly, cupping them like he did before.

Like they are both holding something precious.

Behind Phainon’s head, their constellation shines radiant and proud.

Phainon’s eyes blaze, vulnerable, yet also daring as he says, “Mydei, would you want me to?”

Chapter Summary

For the Cryptogenists, now called the Nousporists, those few who dare to push beyond the limits of academic study, ‘creation’ is a reflection of that mysterious composition they call a ‘soul’.

Few words can describe the difficulties, then, in reconciling these schools of thought to prove—or disprove—that which remains one of Kephale’s most mysterious divine attributes.

author’s notes/content warnings

To wish, despite everything—it is a feeling Mydei has long known.

In his earliest memories, it had been of the most innocent, fervent kind. The frantic gasps of a child tossed about by dark waves in the Sea of Souls. Help me. Save me. Someone, anyone. Each of his deaths had been bracketed by those prayers.

And when each of his deaths were rejected by Thanatos, the first breaths he took were to start them all over again—someone, anyone.

Prayers unanswered until the detachment found him, and the feeling took root, growing fast on its new foundation. His comrades became his shield and blanket as they sang and feasted under the vastness of stars.

Those were halcyon days, when the evernight veil, the black tide, the weight of the crown and throne—all of it became far less intimidating when he knew he was no longer alone.

And when the singing and feasting were done, he’d curl up in the protective middle of his closest friends and let the feeling lull him to sleep as he prayed, let me keep this. Let me stay with them. Let us fight together forever.

Then he lost them. One by one, and the ache in his heart became almost too much to bear. And still the legacy of his people loomed high above. A gilded legacy he chose to set aside, instead taking them away from their ancestral home to the one place that fate had left as his last option.

It was there, before Okhema's gates, that the feeling took on the shape of something like desire.

Desire, when Phainon of Aedes Elysiae met his eyes across the battlefield and smiled. It was an imperfect smile that showed too much teeth, crooked on one side. Smeared with golden blood, though Mydei couldn't tell whether it was the man’s or his own.

An imperfect smile, cracking past the Deliverer’s facade as he grinned at Mydei on the dawn of the tenth day and raised his sword again. He smiled like that at Mydei alone, and no one else.

I want you to always smile like that. A terrible thing for a future king to demand, even in the privacy of his own mind, of a man he barely knew and could ask nothing of.

I want you to always smile at me. Even more selfish a wish. Unbecoming of a Crown Prince; moreso to ask it of the one person blessed and burdened to bring Amphoreus to the new dawn.

Phainon of Aedes Elysiae was not his to keep.

So Mydei had not asked. Had not made it a possibility to himself. He tampered down the wave of emotion whenever Phainon spoke with him, puzzled him, infuriated him, challenged him, won and lost against him and still had the audacity to smile regardless of the outcome.

As if victory and defeat were the same thing to him. Or rather, victory or defeat was not the point.

It would have been easier, or far less complicated, if Phainon did not inspire desire in Mydei as easily as breathing.

I want to know more about your home and your people. Phainon's gaze, cast far over the horizon when he thought no one was looking. Somewhere to a place that Mydei could not find on any map, that Phainon held closer to his heart than anything else.

I want to help shoulder your worries and troubles. A particularly difficult Council meeting that made golden threads tremble in outrage and Phainon's jaw clench for days afterward, unwilling to speak of it despite Mydei waiting for him.

I want you to take care of yourself for once, damn it. As the black tide encroached, and their missions became more dangerous, yet still shouldered with a smile far too bright, too out of place with the golden blood spilled to carry them out.

"I want you," Mydei did not say.

He did not say it even when it became natural for them to step into place beside each other as the Flame-Chase hurtled toward its destiny. Even when the years in Phainon's company made Mydei believe in a future where the end of the west wind will greet them kindly.

“I want you at my side, always,” he kept behind gritted teeth, in the palms of his fists.

Such a wish stood antithesis to the Flame-Chase to which Phainon was so devoted. He could not do it—to insist upon such selfishness when Strife was Mydei's burden to bear. He would not make Phainon lose a husband when duty would eventually call Mydei to arms.

Perhaps, in the tomorrow that was promised, they wouldn’t have reason to lose each other at all.

Then the Trailblazers came, and everything moved so fast, and all the things Mydei wanted were forged into stepping stones for the new dawn.

He was glad for it, would make the sacrifice again and again without regret.

Because the new dawn gave them Era Nova, and the truth of their world, and the universe unfolding like an endless map to be charted.

It gave him Phainon.

Phainon, falling into his arms. Phainon, radiant and divine as the fated cycles shattered like crystal rain around them. In the light of that first new morning, he was smiling fearless and free and everything Mydei ever wanted for him.

Ethereal, for whom the Miracle of Genesis bloomed and bore Amphoreus to the Cosmos.

“Found you,” Phainon had said.

At that moment, Mydei wanted, more than anything. More the five great virtues. More the meaning of the word itself. More than code, and what was written in the stars for him.

“Keep me,” Mydei said. “Stay with me.”

And Phainon—

—Phainon met him in the middle, as he always did, as Mydei always wished for him to.

So, Mydei thought he knew what it meant to wish, despite everything. Despite the odds. Because of them. It was his blessing to have all its meanings be subsumed into his husband, one he guards fiercely and proud for it.

But as Phainon looks at him now, star-drenched and expectant, Mydei realizes that he knew little of the feeling, after all. That there can be so much more to it than he allowed himself to hope for.

Would you want me to?

The words seem to echo around them, this place that was the cradle of their world.

It could be the cradle of something else, if.

If—

Phainon presses Mydei's palms firmly on his abdomen. His eyes shimmer in the lights of a thousand galaxies.

A thousand galaxies could not compare to the multitude of wishes that Mydei barely holds himself back from making.

“My, my,” Phainon husks. “What's this? Has my husband been so bested by a simple question that he can't even look at me?”

He wanted to talk to Phainon about this, did he not? Longed for when they would reunite, so they could speak on the matter together.

But when faced with Phainon being the one to bring it up—

Any explanation, any excuse suddenly seems so paltry.

Phainon cups his cheek. Mydei leans into the touch, shuts his eyes at the roughness of Phainon's palm.

“You don't know what you ask.”

“Oh? I think I was quite clear.” Phainon shifts. The hard panes of his abdomen flex. Could they really soften and give way, to make room for—“Mydei,” Phainon says above the shell of his ear, “Would you want me to bear a child, if I could?”

Mydei's hands seize, clamping down on Phainon's waist. I want I want I want—

Phainon chuckles, a tad shaky, and says, “How does the saying go? Actions speak louder than words?”

Of course they do. Mydei knows that better than anyone. He tips his head and buries his face in Phainon's chest, breathing in his scent. Long fingers rake through his hair, tug at his braid.

Phainon's heartbeat is a steady pitter-patter, faster than usual.

Ah. So Mydei isn't the only one affected. There is something else his husband is not saying. Something he is covering up by redirecting attention to Mydei.

Luckily, Mydei knows him well enough to know how to play along.

“Would, could,” he says, sharpening his focus. “Why do you speak in hypotheticals?”

Phainon noses along his temple. “It might be because I'm working with a hypothetical situation.”

“Being, if you could get pregnant.” He chooses the word deliberately.

Phainon's pulse jumps. Mydei is attuned to it, a lion on the hunt.

“Well,” Phainon says, drawing it out. “If someone as smart as a Genius thought I could, don't you think it's interesting to talk about?”

“So she did think you could,” confirms Mydei, resting his chin on Phainon's clavicle. “You never mentioned what her response was after you brought the possibility up to her.”

Phainon's cheeks turn rosy. “I think it’s a logical deduction based on the questions she asked me.”

“The symptoms she mentioned could have been because of anything else,” Mydei points out. “Your rhimágmata. Kephale's divinity.” Their bodies may have been reforged anew in Era Nova, but Phainon's body still carries the weight of millions of cycles. He closes in. “Why did you think of pregnancy first?”

Phainon's mouth opens, but nothing comes out.

Mydei meets his eyes and challenges, “Is it because you wanted it to be an option?”

“Mydei,” Phainon says weakly.

There it is, so close. Mydei pushes on. His own heartbeat thunders in his ears. “Did you want to hear someone else say it before you brought it up to me?”

Phainon's pupils are blown wide. His hands turn hot on Mydei's shoulders. The mark of the sun flashes. A twitch of his wings is Mydei's only warning before he feels Phainon tense, like a bird about to take flight.

“No you don't,” he growls, and pitches them forward. Phainon lands on his back with a gasp. Mydei arches over him, clamping his thighs tight around Phainon's hips. Another push and a smooth slide, and he pins Phainon’s flailing hands beside his head.

“Going somewhere, husband?” he drawls.

Phainon tries to buck him off, but Mydei rides the movement easily. Phainon hisses, flushed, “What are you doing?”

“Trying to have a conversation,” he replies. “Which was going well until you tried to escape.”

“I didn't—!”

He raises a brow. Phainon purses his lips and looks away.

A win in Mydei's favor. Mydei lets him pout, then eases himself down to the side. He pulls Phainon over so they're facing each other. Phainon keeps his eyes somewhere below Mydei's chin.

Mydei drinks him in: the furrowed set of his brows, the way he nibbles his bottom lip, how his throat works and his fingers squeeze Mydei's again and again as if trying to ground himself in the motion.

He is so painfully lovely against the backdrop of stars.

It's absurd, how quickly Mydei is convinced to break the silence first.

“Let us speak candidly," he says, slow so as to not spook him again.

Phainon nods, eyes still averted.

Mydei presses gently, “Is it possible for you to carry a child?”

Phainon's long lashes flutter. When he finally answers, he is so quiet that Mydei has to strain to hear, “I think it’s possible.”

Mydei takes the end of Phainon's braid, thumbing it to steady his shaking fingers. “How?”

Phainon watches his fingers. “Between divinity and Destruction, our bodies are new. I have my wings. You can still summon your thymós. Anything is possible, at this point.”

Mydei's eyes flick down. Phainon pinches the skin of his palm and whisper-shouts, “Mydei! Nothing's changed there! It's more of intuition. A feeling. I think I could, if I wanted.”

Inside Mydei, something clicks into place, like a key unlocking a door. It swings open, but he can't take a step forward. Not yet. Not without Phainon. “Would you?” he asks.

Phainon shivers all over. He shuffles closer and presses his forehead into Mydei's shoulder.

“Won’t it be dangerous?” Phainon says. The words flow out of him faster now. “Carrying a child—I don't know how my body will handle it. And there's still so much we have to do for Okhema. For Amphoreus. Is now the right time?”

Mydei turns the non-answer over in his mind, parsing through what went unspoken. “Let me rephrase. Would you want to, if you could?”

Phainon burrows deeper into the meat of Mydei's shoulder, still clinging to his hand.

“Phainon?”

Phainon tenses. Mydei can see the thoughts tumbling over themselves in his husband's head. He understands it—the hesitance to have someone perceive him so deeply, because hope can be as strong as steel and as easily snuffed out as a candle flame.

Mydei lifts himself up on an elbow and leans over Phainon, brushing away the hair covering his ear.

“Won't you tell me,” he says, tender at how Phainon shudders in anticipation, “Khaslana?”

My soul knows yours, there is nothing to hide from me.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon whispers. “You’re playing dirty. You can't just use my name like that.”

“I consider it necessary for this circumstance,” he tells him. “Otherwise you'll never tell me what’s on your mind.”

Phainon makes a low, almost chagrined sound before muttering, “That's because it depends.”

“Depends on what?”

“Depends on if you want it, also. A child.”

Blue eyes peer up at him through long lashes, searching. Bright in their clarity. Time yields, and the world suspends in vibrant starry hues.

Also, Phainon said.

Also, meaning, you are not alone.

Also, because I, too, wish for—

Mydei releases Phainon's hand and cups his face, tipping it up to look at him fully.

“I want them to have your eyes.” He touches the slack line of Phainon's mouth. “And your smile.”

Phainon seems to tremble as he reaches for Mydei. “That's funny,” he says, smiling crookedly, widely. “I was just thinking the same thing.”

Only Phainon could make it so easy for Mydei to believe in the impossible. To make it come true.

“I want two,” he bursts out. Phainon's hands are hot, roaming over his eager body. Lips follow and chase Mydei's honesty, which he gives without restraint. “Or three—or four, if you want. If we can.”

He can be greedy this time, can’t he? Can be selfish in front of his husband, and know he won’t be turned away or shamed for such a wish? Can bare his neck, reveal his vulnerable underbelly, lay his desires before Phainon and not be afraid, for he knows they will be reciprocated in full?

Phainon laughs in answer. The Vortex shimmers with it, coming to life in a bloom of colors as if celebrating. This world loves him just as much as Mydei loves him.

“We can,” Phainon says, thick with emotion. “Mydei, we can.”

Later, much later, Mydei traces the halo on Phainon's sternum with his lips and murmurs, “When?”

Phainon plays with the ends of his hair, sifting through the sweaty strands with gentle fingers. “There were mentions of it in the other cycles,” he says sleepily, “but only as a joke. The title Worldbearing lends itself to it, doesn't it?”

Mydei snorts, recalling the debacle in the baths. “So I've learned.”

Phainon hums. “I like it. Taking care of the little ones in Okhema. The Kremnoan children, too. They remind me of the kids back in Aedes Elysiae.”

Mydei drops a kiss on the mark of the sun.

Phainon says wistfully, “I saw how you were with them, back in Okhema. You taught them, trained and played with them. So fair and kind. I always thought you would be a good parent, like your mother.”

Now that. That makes Mydei's chest squeeze tight. He has never sought validation for the way he tried to not be like Eurypon after Strife's madness took him. To be more like Gorgo, in what little ways he could.

Hearing it from Phainon feels like he’s seen in a new light, seen to the core of him.

“You would be a good parent, too,” Mydei says. Even Destruction could not remove love from Phainon's very being. “But you would be far less strict with them, I'd wager.”

“Ah,” Phainon sighs, sounding content. “As if we both won't spoil them rotten.”

Mydei is dozing when Phainon, tucked into his side and still breathing heavily from their last bout, says, “I truly didn't think about it until you brought me that basket from Demetria. I thought you knew those herbs are usually given to expecting or nursing mothers.”

Mydei groans, remembering what Phainon told him about the cremni pear. Maternal origin, he himself had said. The answer was there from the start. Had Demetria already suspected it from that moment? Truly, speculation traveled quickly among Okhema's citizenry.

He musters the strength to tell Phainon everything: about the Trailblazers, the baths, the misunderstandings. By the end of it, Phainon is laughing so hard that tears bud at the corners of his eyes.

“It’s good to know the people care,” Phainon wheezes. “A fight in the baths! Did someone really throw a sandal? An entire fruit platter? What face did Krateros make, again?”

“Do not make me repeat the story, Deliverer.”

Phainon shakes. “Someone said you were infertile,” he howls before breaking down in another fit of laughter.

Mydei scowls and rolls them over. “I'll show you infertile—!”

After, he points to their constellation. “That one is ours.”

“Huh?” Phainon slurs, boneless in the afterglow. Heat radiates from him as he props himself up, following Mydei's finger. “What is?”

Mydei, momentarily distracted by the slick stretch of Phainon's body, gives himself a shake and says, “The constellation. We made it.” He can't help but puff his chest. “It's our creation. Some of the people were right.” Protective instinct wells. “We’ll have to discuss more counter-measures against people claiming it as their own.”

“What are you talking about?” Phainon says, puzzled. He tilts his head. The fine line of his neck becomes very appealing.

Mydei does not give up (there is no word for giving up in the Kremnoan language) but he does set the matter aside in favor of a more pressing task.

“Ask Anaxagoras when we get back,” he says instead, sliding a hand down Phainon’s flank.

“What does Professor Anaxa have to do with… Ah, Mydei, again? I can't—“

“You can,” Mydei says, and proceeds to smugly, thoroughly prove his point.

“Mydei.”

“Mm.”

“Four, really?”

“Too many?”

“We don't even know if we can handle one.”

“What if it's twins?”

“Twins! How ambitious, husband mine. You truly are thinking ahead. I suppose there's little we can do, if it's twins.”

“Then, what if it's triplets?”

“Now you're pushing it. How am I supposed to carry triplets?”

“… with practice?”

“Hahaha, is this still a hypothetical situation?”

“You said anything is possible.”

“Possible, yes. Feasible is another thing. The logistics of it…”

“Children enjoy being around each other, Deliverer. It will be good for them to be playmates and grow together.”

“Yes, but can you imagine raising two or three at the same time? Or me carrying two or three at once? How will I be able to move like that?”

“…”

“Mydei? Why are you looking at me like that? Hey, Mydei, what are you—whoa—!”

Later on:

“You brute, my back hurts.”

“My apologies.”

“Could you be any more blasé? There was not a single hint of sincerity in that sentence.”

“Nor was there any hint of regret in yours.”

“Hah. You'll have to do more than that to make me regret anything.”

“If you're issuing another challenge, I'd be happy to oblige.”

“…”

“That’s what I thought.”

“So what happened after?”

Phainon, drawing lazy, nonsensical shapes through the fresh sweat on Mydei's pectorals, hums questioningly.

“At the Station. After meeting with Herta.” He should have asked sooner about what led Phainon to be in such a state upon coming home, but Phainon doesn't seem to take offense at the delay.

“She ended the session early,” he explains. “Caelus and Sunday snuck me and Tribios out to explore the lower decks. It was quite fun. We should go there sometime, when we’re allowed on the Station together. We fell asleep watching the stars.”

“On the floor?”

Phainon chuckles. “Mr. Yang brought sleeping bags and blankets and kept guard over us. Sunday fell asleep right away. Caelus kept giggling about that for some reason.”

“Hm.” Mydei had seen the Express's Welt Yang in action when the Battle for Amphoreus was raging. He was experienced and steady. Anyone would rest easy with him around.

Mydei will have to send him a token of thanks later, for the protection given over Tribios and his husband.

“Then in the morning?” he prompted.

Phainon clicks his tongue. “We found out a lot of new people were visiting the Station. Scholars and the like. Most of them weren't Madam Herta's. I think they came from other planets.” He drops his head in the crook of Mydei’s neck. “They kept mentioning 'my condition', asking me about it. I was fine the first few times but—” he cuts himself off.

“It became overwhelming,” Mydei fills in.

He can easily imagine it: the suffocating press of dozens of strangers around Phainon and Tribios, in a place far from the familiarity of Amphoreus; how his husband's instincts to protect would rise and ultimately conflict with his desire to maintain peace with others, stranger or not.

“It got so loud,” Phainon confesses. “I couldn’t hear myself think, and I felt like my body was burning up. No one would speak plainly. I thought they meant the rhimágmata. I could never have known they meant pregnancy, of all things!”

No wonder he was so upset. Mydei runs a reassuring hand down his back. “There were so many of them," Phainon sighs. “Then Tribios and Caelus nearly got separated from us, and, well. It was a good thing the other Nameless were there to intervene. I may have said some choice words, though.”

“Good,” says Mydei viciously. He's more than indulgent of Phainon defending his boundaries. “Choice words are the least they deserve.”

Phainon laughs, clearly scandalized and pleased in equal measure. “Ah, Mydei. Maybe it was a good thing for them you weren't there. What if your crystals broke the Station a second time?”

“Like the first time, I will take responsibility but I refuse to be blamed for it,” Mydei tells him. “That's how I am when I have someone precious to protect.”

The few poets of Castrum Kremnos would have shaken their heads, mortified. But it’s worth it, to have Mydei's only equal kiss him passionately, wholly, freely.

“We should probably head back,” Phainon mumbles into their makeshift bed of capes and clothes which desperately need a good wash. His wings have been recalled, leaving the broad expanse of his back tantalizingly bare. “It's been a few days, hasn't it?”

“Three, not counting today.” Mydei stretches and grunts with satisfaction as his joints pop, leaving behind a languid satisfaction. Passion sated and contented for now.

“Three days,” Phainon repeats. He looks over his shoulder, grinning. “Do you think the others are worried?”

“No. I am here with you.” Mydei watches his husband stretch with an appreciative eye. His eyes linger on the curves of Phainon’s waist, his belly. He gives in, nipping the hip closest to him.

Phainon swats at him. A gust of wind would have more force. “Don't start what you can't finish,” he chides.

“Who can't finish,” mutters Mydei, but complies. They have put off returning for long enough. He does not dare to imagine the mountains of work waiting for them when they get back, courtesy of a vindictive Aglaea.

As is her right; he and Phainon are supposed to be helping her with the rebuilding, after all.

“We should bathe,” Phainon says, picking up his undershirt. “Let's go back to our rooms first? I want to see the chimeras.”

“They're probably with Cas.” When he and Phainon are away, the chimeras' first choice of a sitter is almost always Castorice. A stray memory prickles at the back of his mind. “By the way, do you think Beagle Coconut—”

“Hm?” Phainon moves to stand. He makes a soft, startled sound. Seems to freeze, as if his body has locked in place. He sways and tilts to the side.

Mydei rushes to catch him. “Phainon,” he says, horrified at the pale sheen that's come over Phainon. Scarlet crystals grow and sparkle on the ground.

“Mydei,” Phainon says, voice strange and confused. The mark of the sun pulses. “Something feels different.”

His hand moves to his stomach.

“Hyacine!” Mydei roars, stumbling into the Twilight Courtyard. His head spins from the pressure of Space Anchor travel but he refuses to stop and rest.

Hyacine and Stelle jump up. A delicate tea set on the table between them rattles. At Hyacine's feet, Little Ica lets out a sharp doot-doot. It's early morning, and the bustling courtyard comes to a standstill. Dozens of widened eyes turn to him.

Mydei can only imagine the sight he must make: haphazardly dressed with no gauntlets, hair mussed and undone; carrying a sweating and shivering Phainon wrapped up in their capes.

Stelle curses and rushes over to them, teleslate already in hand. Hyacine starts giving out orders. The courtyard snaps into action, attendants full-on sprinting to carry them out.

“Is he injured?” Stelle asks, urgent.

“He fell over in the Vortex.” He feels ice-cold and blazing hot, as if his body can't decide how to react to his husband rendered so weak in his arms. “We were just about to return. He was —I don’t—”

“Mydei,” Hyacine says calmly. He blinks at her, heart threatening to break out from his ribcage.

“I don't know what happened,” he says, throat clogged with simmering panic when Phainon groans in his arms. Little Ica sniffs at Phainon, wings aflutter. Stelle looks like she's been punched.

Hyacine hides her worry well except for where the corners of her mouth pinch tight. “Let's bring him inside.”

Mydei follows at her heels to a small private room in a secluded hall. The curtains are drawn. Several attendants come in with baskets of cloths and jars of medicinal concoctions.

As Hyacine directs the attendants and Stelle taps a blur on her teleslate, Mydei carefully lays Phainon on the kline in the middle of the room.

“Mydei,” Phainon says, weary. His vigor has dissipated like smoke, pallor making the rhimágmata stand out more. He lifts a hand. Mydei catches it and presses his lips to the knuckles.

“I’m here,” he says. It makes Phainon smile. The tiniest sliver of relief cuts through the heavy, tight knot in Mydei's chest.

Before Era Nova, he and Phainon rarely incurred injuries serious enough to warrant a visit to the Twilight Courtyard. Golden blood has its boons, and Nikador and Kephale's divinities granted their own form of immunity against nearly all illnesses.

So when Phainon spasms and pitches over the other side of the bed, retching, Mydei is helpless to do anything but hold him.

“—alert the others as well,” Hyacine is saying somewhere behind him. She comes to Mydei's side. “Tell me everything,” she commands.

Mydei does. Hyacine is professional enough to wave off his stumbling explanations on the more intimate details. She raises her hands over Phainon's body, divine power flaring from her fingertips in rainbow colors.

Phainon cracks one eye open. “Hyacine?” he mumbles. “What's happening?”

Hyacine bites her lip. She glances at Mydei. “Is it okay if you can stand outside with Stelle for a moment? I have to do a full-body examination, and Little Ica and I need the space.”

The last thing he wants is to get in the way of her work. Still, letting go of his husband is a painful endeavor in more ways than one. He squeezes Phainon's hand, only mildly reassured when he squeezes back and sinks into the kline with a labored sigh.

“I got you,” Stelle chimes, and guides Mydei out to the hall.

Mydei does not realize he is sitting and staring at the closed door until Stelle fills his sight. She squats in front of him.

“Hey.” She snaps her fingers lightly to get his attention. “Mydei, hey. It's going to be okay.”

“I have never seen him like that.” It comes out wounded.

“He'll be fine,” she says. “We'll make sure of it.” Her voice takes on the slightest reverb, a touch of the preternatural. She suddenly seems older, more mature.

Mydei knows a little of the Stellaron split between her and Caelus. How mighty and how dangerous it is. The divided views on how to handle its power. The twin Trailblazers are believed by many to be harbingers of cosmic ruin.

But he believes in them, in the indomitable willpower of the Nameless. More than anything, he trusts them. He sucks in a breath and nods, bracing his elbows on his knees.

“Do you think it's Destruction?” asks Stelle.

“If it is, it's a new effect.” Even at his weakest after Era Nova, Phainon never almost collapsed like he did today.

Stelle frowns. “I didn't feel any remnants on him. He looks like he's in the middle of a really bad cold. I got one, back on the Luofo. It was awful.”

“Let it be a cold, and nothing worse.” If anything, it is something Mydei can work with.

The minutes pass, slow as a slog through mud. No sound escapes the room. Stelle paces back and forth. After several turns, she sighs and sits with her legs crossed next to Mydei.

It reminds him of when she waited for him at the Grove. He pats down his pocket and is relieved to take out the braided grass.

“You still have it!” Stelle exclaims, cheery. She cocks her head. “Oh, um, it's a little squished.”

A little squished is putting it generously. The poor braid looks like it went through a Coreflame trial. It’s uneven, fraying and stretched, with one end bent awkwardly in the other direction.

“I'm sorry.”

Stelle shrugs. “You kept it. That's what matters. But geez, did you use it as a training dummy and give it a good pounding or something?”

Strife. Mydei resolutely does not meet her eyes. Clothes had not exactly come flying off the first few times in the Vortex. The braid was in his pocket the whole time.

Stelle covers her mouth. “Mydei. Dude. My good sir.”

“Say nothing.”

“That's why you and Phainon disappeared for three days!?”

“Why do you sound so surprised?” he demands, shoving the braid back into his pocket.

“I'm not! I'm just—I mean, if that little thing looked like that after three days—”

“Stelle!”

“Just sayin', no wonder Phainon looked so worn out—”

Mydei is both grateful and surprised when he hears a slew of voices at the end of the hall, followed by Caelus and Sunday striding into view.

“Cae!” Stelle runs to her twin, who catches her mid-run with a bemused expression. “Sitrep, sitrep. No, don't go near Mydei yet. Trust me.”

A more composed Sunday side-steps the twins. His wings flick as he places a hand over his heart and bows. “Mydeimos. Stelle sent word of Phainon's condition. I thought to accompany Caelus and provide aid.”

“Your support is welcomed,” Mydei says, Aglaea’s courtesy lessons kicking in as he tries to match the Halovian’s formal tone. “Is your Harmony like her powers?”

“In a way,” demurs Sunday. “I am able to sense certain dissonances in one’s energy and help dispel or ward against them.”

“Phainon told me that's what you did for him at the Station. You have my thanks.”

Sunday hesitates. His brow furrows. “About that, when we were there—”

“—you are!” Dan Heng says, skidding around the corner. He is breathing hard. “You two could have waited a little longer. March and Mr. Yang are on their way. Hello, Mydei. Stelle, why are you smiling like that?”

“The crew is coming here?” Mydei says, dumbfounded, at the same time Stelle cries, “At least give me a hello too, Dan Heng!”

“It was a unanimous decision,” replies Sunday, not distracted by Dan Heng’s “Hey!” as he’s dragged into the twins’ huddle. “Pom-Pom remains on the Express, and Himeko and Welt will swap every other hour until we can be sure of Phainon's condition.”

There is the rapid thudding of more footsteps, and the hall bursts with color and noise. The other Heirs pour into the space with Castorice leading at the front with Tribios and Cipher behind her. Upon seeing Mydei, she lights up and waves eagerly.

Anaxagoras steps out from behind her.

“To the soul,” he hisses. A gust of metallic wind and brilliant green light crackle over the impromptu reunion. Mydei finds himself frozen in place as Anaxa advances with a wicked gleam in his eye.

“Crown Prince, what did I say about consequences?”

“Professor Anaxa!”

“Holy shit!”

“Hahaha, where's the Goldweaver? Can you imagine the look on her face when she sees this —”

“Dan Heng, do something or Sunday's gonna end up a roast chicken—”

“Naxy, let De go!”

“Stelle, put your teleslate away and help me—”

The walls shake like the heavens descending in one fell swoop. There's a cacophony of shouts and gasps and curses in multiple languages. Powers and weapons are summoned in flashes of light and fluctuating temperatures. Caelus's lance somehow ends up in the ceiling.

As one, they turn toward the source of the eldritch sound.

Little Ica stares balefully from the open door.

“Thank you, Little Ica,” Hyacine says sweetly. She puts her hands on her hips. “All of you need to be quiet, please!” she scolds. “Professor, you do know that Phainon will be very upset if anything happens to Mydei. And Mr. Sunday, can you come with me? I need a second opinion.”

They stare at her, no one daring to speak first.

“Of course,” Sunday whispers. He slips into the room in haste.

Mydei, freed of Anaxa's sublimation, regains his balance. “How is he?” he rasps, feeling pinpricks all over. “Can I come in?”

“Not yet, but soon,” Hyacine says not unkindly, not answering either before following Sunday.

Little Ica stays outside the door, looking rather put-off. It is likely the only reason why Anaxa remains on the other side of the hall, arms crossed. Mydei tries very hard not to look in his direction and counts his blessings that Aglaea hasn't yet arrived.

“I thought,” Anaxa says severely, his voice projecting, “you two were going to talk, Mydeimos.”

“We did.”

“It must have been a difficult conversation to last three whole days.”

“It was hard at some points, yes.”

A muffled snicker, quickly stopped by a hushed, “Ow, Dan Heng, I didn't say anything!”

“… I mean there was much to discuss.”

“I have no doubt.”

Quiet.

Then, “Little Prince, you must've done a number on the Deliverer boy this time, eh? It's gotta be real serious for Prof Nax to get this worked up.”

“Cifera!”

“Oh it's fine Princess Homebody, someone has to say the truth. Otherwise what are we waiting here for?”

“Whatever it is, I'm sure Phainon will pull through—”

They all jump when the door swings open.

“Mydei,” Hyacine says, tone level. “You can see him now.”

Mydei is in the room before she finishes speaking.

“What's wrong?” he asks. It has been so long since he felt true fear that he almost doesn't recognize it, churning in his gut and rising to the back of his throat. “Is he sick?”

Phainon's tired voice floats from the kline. “He is right here, waiting for his husband to come sit beside him already.”

Tension drains out of his shoulders. He sighs and takes a seat. “If you've found the strength to jest, then perhaps this isn't such a serious ailment after all.”

Some of Phainon’s color has returned, and his eyes are luminous and clear. There's an odd restrained quality to his expression, like he's holding something back.

Across the kline on Phainon's other side, Mydei notices Sunday and Hyacine glancing at each other. He becomes aware of the stillness in the room, a breath held in anticipation.

“What?” he says, taking Phainon's hand. It's warm to the touch, the pulse strong.

Phainon entwines their fingers and, ever so gently, brings them to his lower belly.

Mydei’s thymós lifts its head, called to attention by a deep, primal instinct. He looks from their hands back to Phainon, mouth suddenly dry.

“Hyacine, Sunday, if you would?” Phainon says.

Hyacine bobs her head so fast it looks like it hurts, each bounce sending a burst of rainbow sparkles into the air. Sunday’s wings flutter before they cover his mouth, hiding the hint of a smile.

They extend a hand over Phainon’s and Mydei’s.

“The future will be bright,” Hyacine says like a promise, an invocation, “for we who fly into twilight.” Radiant light spills from her palm onto their hands. It is warm and soft, like being enveloped by sunset clouds.

Sunday's pitch drops into something almost otherworldly, pristine and elegant, as he intones, “Haven in palm, grant thy exalted sweep." His halo and irises glow. “Resonance.”

An indescribable sound like faint music fills the room. Under Mydei’s hand, where Phainon has it splayed out, he feels it.

The stirring of creation. Small, near miniscule. But there. Real.

His knees hit the floor as he abandons the seat to come closer. “Phainon.”

Phainon says, with devastating warmth, “It looks like we’re getting both of our wishes. What say you to that, Mydei?”

Mydei kisses him.

Sweet and deep and slow. The kind of kiss Mydei usually reserves for the privacy of their rooms. It might have gone on for hours, if not for Sunday and Hyacine both clearing their throats pointedly.

Mydei pulls away from his gasping husband with great reluctance. “How? It’s only been three days.”

Hyacine does not ask him to elaborate. “Actually, the energy signature that Mr. Sunday and I found is several weeks old. Almost a month. There are a few layers around it that feel very new, perhaps formed within the last few days.”

“New layers? Could it be more than one?” Phainon asks, having caught his breath.

Mydei’s head goes slightly fuzzy. Strife and calamity. If they say yes, he might actually faint. The detachment’s celebration would make Okhema shake for days.

Sunday shuffles his feet, a rare break in his composure. “If I may use an analogy, it may be that the—ahem—seed was planted some time ago, but waited for the right conditions to grow. Like a bird waiting for a safe nest before laying its egg.”

Hyacine says, without a hint of shame, “My working hypothesis is that the inordinate amount of sex you two had gave it a push to grow as an act of self-preservation.”

Well then.

Phainon gives Mydei a bemused look. “We should have done that sooner if that’s all it took for me to get pregnant,” he laughs. Happiness is beautiful on him.

Mydei is about to kiss him breathless again when the door crashes open. Its hinges and locking mechanism crumple to the side like paper, and the famed Chrysos Heirs and esteemed Nameless fall over the threshold in a mess of flailing limbs.

“Oh my gods,” Stelle wails from the bottom of the pile, “I knew it! I fucking knew it, I’m so happy for you guys, I need to call the others, Caelus you better pay up or I’ll—”

“Be quiet, Stelle!” scolds Caelus with shiny tears in his eyes. “Don’t you realize they were having a moment—” he dissolves into happy sobs.

“We will pay for the door,” Dan Heng as Caelus weeps into his shoulder. “Congratulations, you two.”

“Snowy!” Tribios chirps and claps her hands, perfectly happy to be squished in the middle of the pile. “We’re all so happy for you and De!”

“Doot doot,” Little Ica agrees magnanimously at the top of the pyramid.

The pile shakes as Anaxa’s voice thunders from somewhere, muffled and unintelligible.

Cipher cackles. “Prof, you know my powers can’t do that anymore. And isn’t this what you and the Goldweaver have been waiting for?”

Castorice, dear Castorice, catches Mydei’s eye with a brilliant, jubilant smile. I told you, she mouths, then mimes a puppy walking. Chimeras. Same.

Of course Beagle Coconut is also pregnant. Honey Fruitcake is going to be insufferable. Mydei accepts it and dips his head, knowing they’ll speak more later.

The pile is pulled apart by no small amount of effort, and everyone falls into place around them. A golden thread opens the window. The place swells with sunlight and a gentle breeze, followed by tears and laughter and the baffling exchange of Balance Coins.

Mydei rests his head on Phainon’s chest, one hand covering his lower belly. They bask in the middle of their family and friends, and greet more who come into the room. At some point, Aglaea takes Anaxa’s seat closer to the kline.

“Did you know from the start?” asks Phainon.

“Nothing was impossible anymore,” Aglaea replies indulgently. “If you and Mydei wanted it, I knew you would find a way.”

Her relaxed features turn solemn. Quietly, she says, “There are already ripples beyond our reach. Everything is going to change.”

The stakes have been raised. They will have to call a formal meeting. Potential threats must be assessed, defenses shored up and allies gathered. The Cosmos waits for no one to be ready.

When Mydei looks at his husband, he sees the same unwavering resolve in Phainon’s eyes that burns inside Mydei like the sun.

“Not everything,” Mydei says. “Not this.”

Under the protective cradle of their hands, their child grows.

When they are alone, Mydei slides into the kline and into his husband’s arms.

Phainon says, “I want to raise them in Aedes Elysiae. At least for a few years. Then I want them to see Castrum Kremnos once the rebuilding is done, especially the library. The world we’ve made—I want them to have the chance to explore it. To fall in love with it, and not be afraid of it.”

Countless cycles unfold from the crest of his voice. The love and the longing, the grief and the victorious triumph.

“They will have it,” Mydei promises. “That and more.”

Phainon murmurs, “Cyrene sent word. The fields are growing back. She says the rivers are starting to flow again. We’ll have to build a new house closer to the village square.” He smiles. “I hope you’re ready, Mydei.”

“I look forward to it,” Mydei says. “A family with you. A lifetime of it.”

To wish, despite everything—it is a feeling Mydei has long known. It now settles at long last, glowing gold like the promise of tomorrow.

Mydei holds Phainon and finally rests.
